best_practice_definition: Supply Chain Risk Management (SCRM) is the identification, and prioritization of supply chain risks followed by coordinated and economical application of resources to minimize, monitor, and control the probability and/or impact of unfortunate events or to maximize the realization of opportunities.

Risk Management Strategies are developed and communicated to reduce or eliminate risks. Commonly used strategies include the following:
- Risk mitigation is a plan to reduce the probability of occurrence or minimize the impact of a risk.
- Risk avoidance is used when the probability of occurrence and potential impact is too high or beyond the threshold limits of the organization’s appetite for risk.
- Risk transfer is used when part or all of the risk can be transferred to another process where it can be better managed or mitigated through less costly actions - Risk acceptance occurs when a risk has a low probability of occurrence and low impact, and the company has a contingency plan that can be easily deployed if the risk occurs.
Risk management strategies may differ by supply chain.

Single-Minute Exchange of Die (SMED) is the practice of reducing the amount of time it takes to change a production line, piece of equipment, or machine from running one product to the next. The ability to rapidly change between products is increasingly important in markets where lot sizes are reducing. In general, there are four focus areas to reduce change over time:

- Eliminate non-essential activities. This includes replacing only essential parts and developing universal parts when possible.

- Prepare and set up as much of the production as possible before moving the task to the production line, piece of equipment, or machine.

- Prepare the die through heating, flushing, calibration, and alignment prior to the changeover.

- Simplify the setup inside the equipment. This includes the use of single- or limited- touch fasteners and auto- or self-aligning pins.

Similar to: Single-touch exchange of die.

Network Prioritization for Risk Identification is the process of prioritizing parts of a supply chain for risk analysis based on the overall risk potential in each portion of the supply chain. Prioritization typically is based on the criticality of the component or product flowing through a portion of the supply chain and the number of sources for the material flowing through that portion of the supply chain.

Self-Invoicing or self-billing is the practice in which a customer generates the invoices for the products or services it consumes from a supplier. The advantage of this process for the company that self-invoices is that reconciliation processes, such as three-way verification prior to payment of invoices, are no longer required. Instead, the reconciliation processes are transferred to the supplier.
A common application of this process is Self-Invoicing for transportation services and materials consumed from supplier-owned or consignment inventory.

Conditions for self-invoicing include

- clear service-level agreements between the supplier and the customer

- clear ways to measure the level and quality at which the services were delivered or the materials were consumed

- defined and agreed processes for record-keeping, reporting, and handling claims

- standards for electronic data communication between the supplier and customer.

Consignment inventory is not a prerequisite for Self-Invoicing. Materials ordered from a master contract may also qualify for Self-Invoicing.

Consignment Inventory is a method of organizing source processes in which the ownership of material transfers is based on a signal further down the supply chain, such as in the Make or Deliver activity. For regular inventory, the ownership transfer usually is triggered by the receipt of materials and the verification of the condition of the materials received. The Consignment Inventory practice is designed to delay the ownership transfer to the completion of an activity, such as assembly, production, or shipment to the customer. Application of Consignment Inventory does not lower the physical inventory by default; it impacts ownership of the inventory. Implementation of Consignment Inventory will free up cash. These inventories, generally of finished goods, are in the possession of customers, dealers, agents, brokers, etc., but remain the property of the manufacturer by agreement with those in possession.

Alternative names: Supplier-Owned Inventory, Vendor-Owned Inventory

Baseline Inventory Monitoring helps to avoid overstock situations, companies should regularly review their baseline inventory levels. Baseline inventory is defined as the lowest stock level that a particular stock keeping unit actually reached during the last 12 months. This means that there will be a baseline inventory for all those items that did not have a stockout. At maximum, the baseline inventory should match the safety stock. If it is significantly higher than the safety stock, the planning parameters and buffers in the system need to be reviewed. To evaluate a whole product range, calculate the total aggregate value of baseline inventory. The metric is expressed as a total value, the number of items affected, and the percentage of overall stock value.

This practice will be most effective in a more stable environment with established products. In a highly dynamic market environment, an important outcome of sales and operations planning will be the setting of strategic buffer stocks for key items. To check whether the buffer stocks are on a reasonable level, baseline evaluation can be used.

Slow-Moving Inventory Monitoring is a regular review of slow-moving inventory levels done by companies to avoid overstock situations. As part of this process, companies should evaluate the financial value, number, and storage costs of those stock-keeping units with stock levels that are higher than their total consumption within the last 12 months. Slow-moving inventory are those inventory items with a low turnover; items in inventory that have a relatively low rate of usage compared to the normal amount of inventory carried.

There are various causes for slow-moving inventory. In most cases, there are constraints in terms of time and quantity of supply, such as minimum lot sizes, constrained equipment, or expected shortages of raw materials, that cause a supply-demand imbalance.

To evaluate a whole product range, calculate the total aggregate value of slow-moving inventory. The metric is expressed as a total value, the number of items affected, and the percentage of overall stock value.

Then, slow-moving items are classified into three reason codes: opportunistic stock, technical (supply) reasons, and market (demand) reasons. Newly introduced items are separated from the measurement.

This practice can be applied for any kind of inventory except newly introduced items.

Kanban is a method of just-in-time production that uses standard containers or lot sizes with a single card attached to each. It is a pull system in which work centers signal with a card that they wish to withdraw parts from feeding operations or suppliers. The Japanese word kanban, loosely translated, means a card, billboard, or sign, but other signaling devices such as colored golf balls have also been used. The term is often used synonymously for the specific scheduling system developed and used by the Toyota Corporation in Japan. Kanban is an inventory replenishment technique in which a material is replenished based on consumption. Today Kanban can be implemented using different technological solutions, but a classic example of Kanban is the two-bin-system. One bin is at the point of consumption, for example, on the factory floor, and the second bin is in the process to be filled and placed behind the first. Once the first bin is depleted, it will be sent to be filled, and the second bin now becomes the first bin.

Here’s an example formula to calculate the bin size for a two-bin system:

Minimum bin size = [Projected consumption per time unit] x [Cycle time to replenish, in time units] / [number of bins]

100 per day x 3 days / 2 bins = 150 items.

This formula does not deal with variations in projected consumption or cycle time, but it illustrates that a Kanban system does not need to be complex. The minimum bin size compensates for the cycle time to refill an empty bin. The number of bins can be increased to reduce the amount of material in each bin.

Example applications of Kanban today use Kanban cards to signal the need to replenish stock at the point of use. This might shorten the cycle time of the process and thus decrease the bin size. It also might create additional packing materials that need to be disposed of. Enterprise resources planning systems can replace physical Kanban cards with electronic signals and dashboards.

Min-Max Replenishment, also known as the order-point system, is an inventory replenishment practice in which purchase requisitions or purchase orders are created when inventory for an item drops below the minimum inventory level. The requisition or order quantity will bring the inventory back to the maximum inventory level. The order quantity is variable and is the result of the maximum minus available or on-order inventory. Min-Max Replenishment methods are generally implemented through automation. Different configuration options exist for Min-Max Replenishment:

Physical Min-Max Replenishment incorporates on-hand inventory; existing customer orders are not included in the calculations. This option has characteristics close to a Kanban system.
Logical Min-Max Replenishment nets customer orders from the on-hand inventory. If this inventory the net of the orders is less than the minimum order quantity, a requisition or order will be created. This aligns with available-to-promise or capable-to-promise practices. Further details may include netting only clean orders or netting all orders. Clean orders are orders that are free of customer holds, credit holds, or other types of holds.

The calculation of the minimum level includes replenishment cycle time and a buffer for variability in demand and cycle times. The maximum level is preferably the minimum level plus economic order quantity.

Generally, Min-Max Replenishment requires process automation. Reordering is triggered by running a replanning program or report.

Production Line Sequencing is the practice in which materials are ordered, shipped, received, and staged in the same sequence as they will be consumed. The materials generally are configurable or have many variants, such as different colors. This practice can be applied in on-site processes and in supplier-to-manufacturer processes:
On-site processes: The materials are picked from an inventory location, such as a raw material warehouse, in the exact sequence of the production schedule or line and delivered to the point of use. The operator is required to use the materials in the sequence they were provided. This can apply to materials sourced using S1, S2, and S3 processes. Supplier-to-manufacturer processes: The materials are ordered from the supplier in sequence. The supplier processes the order and loads the transportation vehicle in sequence. The materials are then unloaded and delivered to the point of use in sequence. This version applies to S2 and S3 sourcing only.

It is important that order managers, material handlers, and operators understand that the materials should always remain in sequence. Accidental sequencing may cause erroneous products, dangerous working conditions, and rework. Example physical implementations include conveyor systems but also the use of trays or bins that allow the materials to be kept in sequence during transportation and handling.

Lot Tracking is the practice of storing information about the history and genealogy of a product or material. This may include where it was sourced, the different materials used to make it, the grade of the materials, and other product genealogy information. Lot Tracking has three fundamental requirements, namely:

- a means to identify the lot or serial number

- a system to record milestones for each lot or serial number

- a process to retrieve information by lot or serial number.

Lot Tracking may make use of bar coding, radio frequency identification tags, or other visual or electronic methods to identify the lot. Modern enterprise resources planning and other specialized supply chain systems generally offer lot recording and display functionality. Hardware and operator or handler instructions may be required to read the lot identifiers and communicate the event or milestone to the recording system.

To establish a Lot Tracking system, it is important to understand what information needs to be collected, where and at what level. The scope of where information is collected may extend beyond the boundaries of an organization to its customers or its customers’ customers. The need for Lot Tracking may be dictated by regulatory requirements, risk mitigation strategies, process excellence initiatives, or customer requirements.

Alternative names: Serial tracking, serial or lot tracking, lot history, lot tracking and tracing, material traceability

Item Rationalization, which also is called stock keeping unit (SKU) or product rationalization, involves decision-making related to adding, deleting, or retaining products, services, or features within a portfolio offering. Some strategies call for these decisions to be made at the product family level. Rationalization should consider at what stage of manufacturing the item becomes customized as well as how close to the customer order the customization should occur to optimize operational costs and limit complexity. Given the multiple factors and tradeoffs implicit in rationalization decisions, Item Rationalization should be considered an element of, but not a substitute for, a more comprehensive supply chain complexity management approach.

Item Rationalization is important throughout the entire product life cycle. After the product introduction process, an item must be periodically reviewed to identify its stage in its life cycle.

A rationalization exercise should identify the most cost-effective way to deliver the product to the market throughout its life cycle while taking into account factors like the cost to serve, margin, sales projections, as well as what other products and services are better enabled by the item.

Demand Planning and Forecasting is the practice of using state-of-the-art forecasting algorithms for product life cycle planning and trade promotion planning.

Understanding and predicting customer demand is vital for manufacturers and distributors to avoid stockouts and maintain adequate inventory levels. Although forecasts are never perfect, they are necessary to prepare for actual demand. In order to maintain optimized inventory and an effective supply chain, accurate demand forecasts achieved through the most advanced algorithms are imperative. The algorithms or mathematical models are the core of demand and supply management solutions. They make it possible to seamlessly work at any level of aggregation and along any dimension such as product, channel, or customer with ease yet without rigid forecast pyramids. Typically, Demand Planning and Forecast is accomplished through the process of combining statistical forecasting techniques and judgment to construct demand estimates for products or services (both high and low volume; lumpy and continuous) across the supply chain from the suppliers’ raw materials to the consumer’s needs. Items can be aggregated by product family, geographical location, product life cycle, and so forth, to determine an estimate of consumer demand for finished products, service parts, and services. Numerous forecasting models are tested and combined with judgment from marketing, sales, distributors, warehousing, service parts, and other functions. Actual sales are compared to forecasts provided by various models and judgments to determine the best integration of techniques and judgment to minimize forecast error.

Success measurement: Forecast accuracy in the supply chain is typically measured using the mean absolute percent error (MAPE). Statistically, MAPE is defined as the average percentage of errors. Most practitioners, however, define and use MAPE as the mean absolute deviation (MAD) divided by average or mean sales. This is, in effect, a volume-weighted MAPE. This also is referred to as the MAD/mean ratio.

A simpler and more elegant method to calculate MAPE across all the products forecasted is to divide the sum of the absolute deviations by the total sales of all products.

Safety Stock Planning enables companies to meet desired customer service levels while maintaining a minimum amount of safety stock.

The standard methods of Safety Stock Planning are used to build stock on hand according to the safety stock values that companies define in their location product master, depending on previous experience. In contrast with model-based Safety Stock Planning, forecast errors are not considered when using the standard methods. Safety stock values can be maintained as static or time-dependent values.

The advanced methods of Safety Stock Planning are used to calculate the time-dependent safety stock for finished products and components. In this type of planning, the system considers the demand forecasts and forecast errors within the supply chain. In general, a quantity of stock is planned to be in inventory to protect against fluctuations in demand or supply. 2) In the context of master production scheduling, the additional inventory and capacity are planned as protection against forecast errors and short-term changes in the backlog. Overplanning can be used to create safety stock.

Supply Network Planning involves simulating and implementing comprehensive tactical planning and sourcing decisions based on a single, globally consistent model. The practice enables organizations to create a very close match between supply and demand by integrating purchasing, manufacturing, distribution, and transportation into one consistent model. By modeling the entire supply network and related constraints, it is possible to synchronize activities and plan material flow throughout the entire supply chain. The results are feasible plans for purchasing, manufacturing, inventory, and transportation.

The process also includes enabling organizations to dynamically determine how and when inventory should be distributed. The supporting system optimizes deployment plans based on available algorithms as well as user rules and policies.

Distribution Planning is a method that helps determine the best short-term strategy to meet demand and replenish stocking locations. Distribution planning activities typically include planning activities associated with transportation, warehousing, inventory levels, materials handling, order administration, site and location planning, industrial packaging, data processing, and communications networks to support distribution.

Distribution Planning enables the user to set certain inventory control parameters, such as safety stock, and calculate the time-phased inventory requirements. This process also is commonly referred to as distribution requirements planning (DRP).

The ABC Inventory Classification System is a Pareto analysis of a range of inventory items, which are classified into three or four inventory categories. The ABC system requires different levels of inventory control for each of the categories. The classification of a group of items in decreasing order of annual dollar volume (price multiplied by projected volume) or other criteria. This array is then split into three classes, called A, B, and C. The A group usually represents 10 percent to 20 percent by the number of items and 50 percent to 70 percent by projected dollar volume. The next grouping, B, usually represents about 20 percent of the items and about 20 percent of the dollar volume. The C class contains 60 percent to 70 percent of the items and represents about 10 percent to 30 percent of the dollar volume. The ABC principle states that effort and money can be saved through applying looser controls to the low-dollar volume class items than to the high-dollar volume class items. The ABC principle is applicable to inventories, purchasing, and sales. A common calculation is the standard cost multiplied by the quantity used per time period.

Demand Management takes Demand Planning to the next level and integrates the plan up and down the supply chain as well as across the enterprise. It takes a holistic view of a multi-unit enterprise, its markets, and its trade partners’ capabilities. Using sophisticated software tools and web technologies, supply chain managers can aggregate demand, manage inventories, and respond in near real-time to changes in demand. Multiple, real-time applications are used within a Demand Management process to analyze and evaluate changes in demand and the impact on supply. Demand Management establishes priorities when supply is lacking and facilitates the planning and use of resources for profitable business results.

In marketing, it’s the process of planning, executing, controlling, and monitoring the design, pricing, promotion, and distribution of products and services to bring about organizational and individual needs.

Centralized systems and applications that are capable of receiving, monitoring, and processing information in real-time from various business unit enterprise resources planning (ERP) systems are used in the Demand Management process. These applications are agnostic of operating systems and ERP applications and can operate as part of the enterprise information technology infrastructure or as a software-as-a-service application.

Sales and Operations Planning (S&OP) is a mid- to long-term supply chain planning practice that seeks to compare the forecast sales plan with the company resources, including production capacity, people, and raw materials, and analyze where any imbalances to the plan might exist.

A process to develop tactical plans that provide management the ability to strategically direct its businesses to achieve competitive advantage on a continuous basis by integrating customer-focused marketing plans for new and existing products with the management of the supply chain. The process brings together all the plans for the business (sales, marketing, development, manufacturing, sourcing, and financial) into one integrated set of plans. S&OP is performed at least once a month and is reviewed by management at an aggregate (product family) level. The process must reconcile all supply, demand, and new product plans at both the detail and aggregate levels and tie to the business plan. It is the definitive statement of the company’s plans for the near to intermediate term, covering a horizon sufficient to plan for resources and to support the annual business planning process. Executed properly, the S&OP process links the strategic plans for the business with its execution and reviews performance measurements for continuous improvement.

S&OP is a strategic tool normally reviewed by the executive or senior management team, which then makes decisions to remove any imbalances. Common actions include making changes to shift patterns, headcounts or inventory policies.

Material Requirements Planning (MRP) is a set of techniques that uses bill of material data, inventory data, and the master production schedule (MPS) to calculate requirements for materials. It makes recommendations to release replenishment orders for material. Further, because it is time-phased, it makes recommendations to reschedule open orders when due dates and need dates are not in phase.

Time-phased MRP begins with the items listed on the MPS and determines

- the quantity of all components and materials required to fabricate those items

- the date that the components and material are required.

Time-phased MRP is accomplished by exploding the bill of material, adjusting for inventory quantities on hand or on order, and offsetting the net requirements by the appropriate lead times.

MRP is a Plan scheme of the different inventory management practices that have been adopted by a company in a mixed-model manufacturing environment. Manufacturing models can include Assemble-to-Order, Make-to-Order or Make-to-Stock, among others.

Business Rule Management is a practice in which business rules in a human-readable form are used by, but not embedded in, supply chain systems. The business rules should be visible, easily modified by non-programmers, and usable by any application and channel.

Business Rule Management formalizes a supply chain's critical business rules in a language that business and information technology staff can understand. Business rules are established to help an organization achieve its goals and are an unambiguous statement to support decision-making. The formal specification of a business rule becomes information for process and rules engines to run.

Supply Chain Optimization (SCO) is a part of the enterprise strategic plan for leading-edge companies. SCO allows top management to redesign the supply chain as part of the enterprise`s overall strategy, typically in response to actual or anticipated changes in the marketplace. Based on actual data or analyst projections, companies run multiple computer simulations to look for an optimal solution for business challenges such as:

- the total number of vendors and their current and prospective locations and inventory levels

- the total number of manufacturing, retail, service, warehousing, and distribution facilities and their prospective locations

- global transportation costs

- product life cycle management

- local, state, national, and international regulations

- carbon footprint and other environmental considerations.

Improvements are planned in a proactive rather than a reactive manner, which provides a financial and velocity advantage over competitors.

Optimized supply chains have shorter cash-to-cash cycles, shorter customer lead times, lower inventory requirements, lower excess and obsolete inventories, and lower transportation costs.

Technology providers offer individual applications and complete sets of optimization software packages in both information technology enterprise and software-as-a-service solutions.

Self-Service Warranty Claim Submittal enables customers and service providers to submit warranty claims through the internet, reducing internal validation and processing workload. This can be accomplished as a batch load of several claims at the same time or as individual claims submitted one at a time. Information captured at the time of submittal helps with further analysis and disposition.

Results of the analysis can be made available online based on login access levels so that the same information can be submitted to appropriate authorities as needed. Furthermore, auto-approval and auto-payment of certain claims can be considered.

best_practice_name: Improve Sales and Operations Planning (S&OP) Process
best_practice_definition: Improve Sales and Operations Planning (S&OP) Process directs supply chain management teams to establish a disciplined, monthly cross-functional process to increase the accuracy of demand management or forecasting, establish a business inventory policy, and reach agreements on demand and supply balancing.

Pull-Based Inventory Replenishment is an approach that utilizes customer demand as the impetus or pull to replace and optimize inventory while also reducing total net landed cost. It has been a widely recognized, effective practice for decades.

With a pull-based approach, the signal to replenish downstream inventory is driven by actual demand or usage, rather than by a forecast that pushes products and materials into the supply chain. Pull-based replenishment uses a methodology that focuses on historical demand variability between forecasted demand versus real customer demand to identify the appropriate inventory levels.

Inventory Optimization is the use of multi-echelon, random optimization. The optimization happens simultaneously across all inventory stocking points in the supply chain, and it accounts for random variability. This practice is traditionally used for the replenish-to-forecast work process as an alternative to pull-based replenishment, but it also can be used to calculate reorder points.

Supply chains and supply networks both describe the flow and movement of materials and information through linked organizations that work together to serve the end customer. Network Optimization can be used to determine optimal manufacturing and warehouse locations based on the goal of reducing total supply chain costs, which typically is based on reducing transportation costs. This is done by reviewing a supply chain network of product-supplying and market-facing businesses to consolidate inventory-stocking locations.

Inventory Record Accuracy is an established, disciplined monthly process to ensure timely reporting of accurate inventory at manufacturing and terminal locations. This involves ensuring that physical inventory matches the inventory counted in the enterprise resources planning system and identifying sitting inventory that is not identified by a stock keeping unit.

best_practice_name: Stock Keeping Unit (SKU) Rationalization and Cost of Sales Analysis
best_practice_definition: Stock Keeping Unit (SKU) Rationalization and Cost of Sales Analysis is an inventory-reduction practice that helps determine which SKUs that can be terminated through a cost of sales analysis. This practice may require working with customers to determine the potential to change to another SKU or to make the decision to abandon a given SKU because of poor sales.

best_practice_name: Reduce or Write Off Slow-Moving Inventory
best_practice_definition: Reduce or Write Off Slow-Moving Inventory is a process for analyzing and determining what inventory can be written off because of age, shelf life, or lack of demand. This practice usually is governed by how much the organization is willing or able to write off based on its reserves and the impact on its financial statement.

Traditional Demand Forecasting Improvement refers to the use of more sophisticated qualitative and quantitative forecasting processes and tools to improve a customer demand forecast, typically at the stock keeping unit level. This would be an improvement on the traditional forecasting process, and it can be combined with additional opportunities, such as sales and operations planning, which uses forecasting modeling.

Collaborative inventory planning can be used as a way to extend supply chain planning with key customers. It can be done through a joint sales and operations planning (S&OP) meeting with each key customer and supplier to discuss how to manage demand and supply across the extended enterprise. These meetings should include reviews of historical and future customer demand, demand forecast accuracy, planned outages by customer or supplier, long-term planning, and other considerations. In collaborative forecasting, the supply chain members jointly maintain and update a single forecasting process in the system. Hence, forecasting information becomes centralized.

Business rules for an organization are the policies or procedures that define or constrain some aspect of the business and are meant to provide guidance. Business Rule Review is performed regularly by an organization’s middle- or upper-level supply chain managers, whether on a weekly, monthly, quarterly, semiannual, or annual basis. In this practice, the manager ensures that the framework for analysis of a business rule is in line with the objectives and strategy of the organization as well as the operational aspects the rule governs. The rule should be clearly defined and linked to the respective business process or processes.

Consignment inventory is a family of business models in which the buyer of a product provides certain information to a supplier of that product and the supplier takes full responsibility for maintaining an agreed amount of the material, usually at the buyer's consumption location. Consignment inventory can be combined with additional opportunities, such as extended inventory planning across suppliers by using collaboration. The intent is to have suppliers carry raw material inventory on their balance sheets until it is consumed.

Manufacturing Direct or Drop Shipment is the practice of shipping products and goods directly from the manufacturing plant to the customer, bypassing consolidation activities in warehouses and distribution centers. In retail, direct shipment, also called drop shipment, is a supply chain management technique in which the retailer does not keep goods in stock. Instead, the retailer transfers customer orders and shipment details to either the manufacturer or a wholesaler, who then ships the goods directly to the customer.

Using direct shipment will bypass a distribution network and may reduce the distribution of finished goods inventory based on customer locations. Direct shipment can be combined with additional opportunities, such as Inventory Management Using Supply Chain Network Optimization (BP.029).

Batch-Size Reduction is the practice of using Lean principles to reduce the size of manufacturing batches to better match customer demand rather than asset utilization or quality issues. Historically, manufacturing companies have operated with large batch sizes to maximize machine utilization, assuming that changeover times were fixed and could not be reduced. Because Lean calls for the production of parts to customer demand, the ideal batch size is one. However, a batch size of one is not always practical, so the goal is to practice continuous improvement to reduce the batch size to the smallest size possible. Reducing batch sizes reduces the amount of work-in-process inventory (WIP) as well as inventory carrying costs. In addition, production lead time or cycle time is approximately directly proportional to the amount of WIP. Therefore, smaller batch sizes shorten the overall production cycle, enabling companies to deliver more quickly and invoice sooner, which results in improved cash flow. Shorter production cycles also increase inventory turns and allow the company to operate profitably at lower margins, which enables price reductions that, in turn, increase sales and market share.

Batch-Size Reduction can be combined with additional opportunities, such as Right Size Frequency of Production Wheel (BP.039) or reorder point production models, which follow pull-based replenishment.

best_practice_name: Right Size Frequency of Production Wheel
best_practice_definition: Rightsized Frequency of Production Wheel refers to the use of Lean principles to increase the frequency and agility of a production wheel or production cycle in order to modify production planning and right size finished goods and work-in-process inventory. This can be combined with Batch-Size Reduction (BP.038) or reorder point production models, which follow pull-based replenishment.

MTO Order Fulfillment Strategy involves evaluating the potential to change an order fulfillment strategy from Make-to-Stock to MTO for a given stock keeping unit to offset the need to carry inventory because of infrequent or low demand. The key here is to also have manufacturing flexibility and agility to be able to make this changeover in a short period of time so that customer demands still can be met. MTO is a production environment where a good or service can be made after receipt of a customer’s order. The final product is usually a combination of standard items and items custom designed to meet the special needs of the customer. Where options or accessories are stocked before customer orders arrive, the term assemble-to-order is frequently used. This practice can be combined with Stock Keeping Unit (SKU) Rationalization and Cost of Sales Analysis (BP.031).

Transportation Optimization involves evaluating the potential to change inbound or outbound transportation modes to faster modes, depending on freight terms, to accelerate the transfer of inventory to customers, to better match supply and demand, and optimize inventory balances. This practice can be combined with additional strategies such as risk pooling and deciding to source from local stocking points to reduce cycle time.

Procurement Terms and Conditions Review involves monthly, quarterly, or annual evaluation of potential changes to procurement contract terms with suppliers to

- focus on potential inventory impacts caused by early deliveries, delivery quality, receipt inspection, vendor-managed inventory, incentives, technology enablement through radio frequency identification and barcoding, and shipment notifications to carriers

- minimize raw material inventory levels

- consolidate internal business purchasing contracts with shared raw material suppliers to one global purchasing contract to leverage global buying power.

This practice can be combined with additional opportunities, such as reducing customer consignment stock or enabling supplier collaboration.

Inventory Financing Evaluation involves evaluating the potential to use an external finance company to purchase inventory that is in transit or in certain circumstances and sell it back to the originating company prior to delivery to the customer. Some of the other larger third-party logistics companies and technology service providers offer this as a value-added service as part of international transportation.

Delay Inbound Supplier Shipments is the practice of analyzing and executing a delay in inbound supplier raw material shipments to reduce raw material costs at summer break, the end of the year, or during another scheduled plant closure. This would defer any additional raw material inventory, based on plant shutdown and restart timing, to only what is absolutely required at a plant location.

Finished Goods Inventory Postponement is the process of determining and executing optimum placement and volume for inventory in the value stream. This practice requires analyzing the value stream, identifying opportunities for demand pooling of materials, and conducting a detailed analysis of required delivery and cumulative lead times as well as manufacturing and logistics capabilities.

This practice can be combined with additional opportunities, such as changing the order fulfillment strategy from Make-to-Stock to Make-to-Order and decoupling point analysis.

Demand Shaping involves the balancing of the cost and value of offering discounts for customers to place orders for specific finished good products in inventory. This practice typically requires processes and tools to identify and analyze the value proposition or trade-off. Organizations may be able to leverage other commercial tools to analyze payment incentives.

Proper predictive models are the key to being able to proactively manage developing problems rather than reactively coping with the missed milestones. Lean Planning creates real-world project plans that robustly model the project from initiation to final delivery.

Beginning with the end deliverable is the best way to create a tactical plan. Lean Planning identifies the information flow between tasks and pushes back this information one task at a time during the planning process. This creates a robust project model that identifies all of the work that must be completed to accomplish the end deliverable of the project.

Design for Logistics (DFL) Management is a part of the new product development process that works to embed reuse and risk assessment into inventory management. The design of products that considers all aspects of a product’s movement and storage pertaining to manufacturing, packaging, shipping, warehousing, merchandising, and repackaging for returns. The chosen design is intended to control logistics costs, increase customer service levels, facilitate ease of transport, and facilitate ease of shelving within distribution centers and stores. Other considerations include environmental impacts and security. For example, DFL Management can include an assessment of the new product’s potential inventory management impact. Such impacts could include ending the life cycle of another product and commercial agreements for potential inventory and working capital exposure.

This also can include taking steps to design outer packaging for the product that will protect the product during storage and transportation while also enabling bulk shipping and supporting efficient cube utilization to unlock transportation and distribution savings. The outer packaging also can be designed to accommodate returned items, if needed.

Manufacturing Reliability Improvement involves the use of reliability tools and the implementation of work process roles within manufacturing to address manufacturing reliability. It incorporates analysis and simulation of the manufacturing process to identify opportunities to increase equipment reliability and improve manufacturing costs, capacity, and service factors.

best_practice_name: Manufacturing Quality Improvements for Return Reduction
best_practice_definition: Manufacturing Quality Improvements for Return Reduction consists of efforts to address manufacturing quality and improve manufacturing cost, capacity, and service factors. This would require analysis or simulation of quality losses and returns as well as opportunities for inventory reduction. Manufacturing Quality Improvements for Return Reduction also includes formulating a process and timeline by which to move off-grade or returned products off the books.

Freight Carrier Delivery Performance Evaluation is the practice of conducting formal freight carrier performance reviews to reduce the risk of landed cost budget variances and poor delivery performance. A formal evaluation is crucial because transportation partners represent the interface between suppliers and customers. The quality of delivery on time and in good condition has enormous impacts on customer satisfaction, return rates and repeat sales

A carrier evaluation program needs a comprehensive list of evaluation metrics to reflect overall service performance and cost-improvement objectives. Evaluation criteria should include quantitative as well as qualitative measures. Quantitative criteria could include on-time delivery performance, claims ratios, billing accuracy, cost performance and other measurable criteria. Qualitative measures may include driver and sales representative responsiveness, the quality of customer service, stakeholder surveys, customer complaints or other value-based assessments.

In addition, a freight carrier’s delivery performance and impact related to supply lead-time variability due to both early and late deliveries should be evaluated. If a product arrives late to a customer, the party does not have the needed amount of inventory. Conversely, if a shipment arrives prior to the need date, then the customer has to carry the excess inventory. To correct these issues, the involved parties should investigate the reasons behind these early and late deliveries, which can include the supplier purposely shipping the product early to move inventory quickly or the receiving company wants to delay shipment until inventory is needed. Then, determine how to better manage such situations, such as by adjusting the transit lead time.

Supplier Raw Material Quality Assurance provides analysis of the potential value that could be gained from raw material inventory reduction. It requires analysis or simulation of the current impact of raw material quality and opportunities for reducing inventory while improving quality.

This practice can be combined with additional opportunities, such as embedding inventory management goals in purchasing.

Inventory Management Training involves developing an inventory management training curriculum and monitoring key employee participation and completion. Key employees typically include schedulers, planners and supply chain managers. Training should also expose key employees to emerging best practices and technologies.

This can be done with existing online training courses as well as trade organization meetings and events.

Unsold inventory ties up money that can't be used for other purposes. A company should use Reduce Non-Strategic Inventory Level to identify idle assets and reduce or sell the non-strategic inventory. This involves analyzing production records and reviewing stock status reports to isolate slow-moving and out-of-balance inventory.

This practice includes selling obsolete and excess inventory by establishing and offering short-term discounts to turn inventory to cash.

Master Data Accuracy requires the regular revalidation of existing master data items, such as those about order lead times, replenishment times, transit times and other factors, to ensure that the data matches current operational capabilities and performance. This information is used in inventory reorder point setting and target setting to determine inventory replenishment size and frequency. This is a critical step in inventory management and requires monthly repetition to provide accurate and reliable information to the number of processes and systems that rely on this information as key input variables. It also is important to establish a clear role, responsibility, and accountability for master data management.

This practice is a critical prerequisite for a wide range of inventory opportunities. It also can be combined with additional strategies, including pull-based replenishment.

best_practice_name: Optimize Sourcing Decisions to Local Source Point
best_practice_definition:
Optimize Sourcing Decisions to Local Source Point is the practice of assessing the potential to source from a local source point, likely the optimal source point, rather than a distant one to reduce overall replenishment lead time. This would reduce both transportation and inventory costs and could impact service-level and revenue objectives, depending on balance demand and supply decisions. Consider using an advanced planning system to optimize sourcing decisions.

This practice can be combined with additional opportunities, such as Network Optimization (BP.029).

Safety stock is a quantity of stock planned to be in inventory to protect against fluctuations in demand or supply. Safety Stock Reduction is the practice of pursuing a more aggressive reorder point or safety stock target replenishment stance that increases the risk of a stockout. This can be done quickly to help mitigate a potential sharp downturn in demand. It also includes evaluating the costs of holding raw materials and the amount of material or supply compared with demand.

This practice can be combined with additional opportunities, such as pull-based replenishment or Inventory Optimization (BP.028).

best_practice_name: Returns Policy to Reduce Returns Inventory
best_practice_definition: Returns Policy to Reduce Returns Inventory involves evaluating and establishing a business returns policy and determining its impact on overall inventory management. The policy should include rules for handling buyer’s remorse, defective items, instances in which the buyer purchased more items than it needed, and items that are covered by warranty as well as a procedure for a root-cause investigation to determine and eliminate the causes of returns. Organizations also should develop plans for reusing or reselling returned items when possible. To determine the policy’s impact, proactively model potential returned inventory levels. Include these models in projected overall inventory levels, and then determine appropriate inventory costing.

Returns Inventory Reduction is the practice of developing a process for efficiently receiving, processing, and disposing of returned products. The cycle time in this returns process can be reduced through the use of an automated enterprise resources planning system.

This practice can be combined with additional opportunities, such as Returns Policy to Reduce Returns Inventory (BP.066).

Supplier Delivery Performance Analysis is the practice of monitoring and evaluating key suppliers on cost, quality, engineering, purchasing, and so on, based on an agreed set of measurements including the on-time delivery performance of suppliers. It is important to take action for large-volume or -value orders of raw materials to ensure that there is no consistent early receipt of raw materials. To support this effort, train planners and manufacturing, and warehouse staff not to accept early shipments. Also, consider penalizing suppliers for early shipments.

Raw Materials Receiving Process is the practice of developing a strategy for efficiently receiving and processing raw materials from suppliers to minimize the amount of time to receive raw materials. Components of this process may include advanced shipping notifications, receiving inspections, bar code label scanning, use of master pack labels, use of shrink wrap, and efficient receiving and put-away procedures.

This practice can be combined with additional opportunities, such as Supplier Performance Reporting (BP.068).

Planning and Scheduling Inventory Training is important for improving employee knowledge of inventory control and inventory management. When employees are more skilled at methods of inventory management, the organization can lower its inventory levels/improve its Inventory Days of Supply (DOS).

Modal Optimization is the practice of balancing the trade-off between logistics cost reduction and increased capital costs. Factors for identifying the dimensional size to minimize freight costs include shipment lot size, per-shipment setup costs, consumption of and demand for raw materials, and storage capacity.

Inbound Return Material Authorization (RMA)–Enabled Processing is a transaction (document) that describes a product return and authorizes the acceptance of returned items. A signatory authorization is normally required to return the goods and has a unique RMA number.

Returns Receiving Refurbishment is the practice of refurbishing materials during the receiving or Source processes for returned materials.

This practice enables shorter processing cycle times through the refurbishment of materials that have been deemed eligible for rework and return. Specifically, when defective materials are returned and processed by the receiving function, repairs, modifications, or enhancements are made by the same receiving personnel, rather than sending the materials to personnel who handle the Transform process elements. Then the materials are sent to the shipping function for return to the original recipient. This practice would only be used for a subset of refurbishment situations, such as for high-volume repair returns or for materials that only require minor modifications and requires additional training for and capabilities from receiving personnel. The benefits of this practice include shorter overall return processing times and reduced capacity requirements from existing assets and processes related to the Transform process elements.

Process and Metrics Alignment refers to the organized and deliberate development of metrics across an organization. The process starts with developing organizational, business, or supply chain metrics and then moves to developing metrics for organizational processes and more specific levels if desired.
Bar Coding is a method of encoding data using bar codes for fast and accurate readability.

More and more companies are providing Prepaid Return Shipping Labels and instructions for return at the time a product is sold and shipped to the customer. Common examples include instructions for returning an item if the customer is not satisfied with it or instructions for sending in an empty container, such as an ink cartridge, for a refill. In these cases, the return freight cost has been pre-negotiated, the original shipping package can be reused for the return, and the return label is coded with a tracking number for further tracking via the transportation company.

Return Tracking allows customers to track their return shipment by using the tracking number assigned by the carrier when they are returning a product. If the same information is provided to the vendor during the return material authorization process, the receiving department can better plan for the receipt of the returned product.

Enterprise Performance Management is the process of monitoring performance across the enterprise with the goal of improving business performance. An EPM system integrates and analyzes data from many sources, including e-commerce systems, front- and back-office applications, data warehouses, and external data sources. Advanced EPM systems can support many performance methodologies, such as the balanced scorecard.
Continuous Improvement is the act of making incremental, regular improvements and upgrades to a process or product in the search for excellence.

Project Management is the use of skills and knowledge in coordinating the organizing, planning, scheduling, directing, controlling, monitoring, and evaluating of prescribed activities to ensure that the stated objectives of a project, manufactured good, or service are achieved; aka project.

Inventory Cycle Counting is an inventory accuracy audit technique where inventory is counted on a cyclic schedule rather than once a year. A cycle inventory count is usually taken on a regular, defined basis (often more frequently for high-value or fast-moving items and less frequently for low-value or slow-moving items). Most effective cycle counting systems require the counting of a certain number of items every workday, with each item counted at a prescribed frequency. The key purpose of cycle counting is to identify items in error, thus triggering research, identification, and elimination of the cause of the errors.

Supply Network Planning is the integrated planning of all products of a supply chain at all relevant locations. Supply Network Planning attempts to fulfill all demand by considering all relevant constraints. For fulfillment, Supply Network Planning assigns available inventory, propagates demand to sourcing locations, finds substitute products, and explodes bills of materials (BOMs). Using material requirements planning (MRP) logic, Supply Network Planning creates corresponding orders for supply, such as purchase requests, purchases, transportation orders, or production orders.

Supply Network Planning can consider constraints such as available location inventory; inventory reservations; preferred vendors; preferred production sites; minimum inventory levels; preferred routings; BOMs; and durations for sourcing, production, material handling, and transportation between locations.

In case of shortages, Supply Network Planning can consider priorities between different types of demand, such as more or less important orders from customers, demand from the forecast, or replenishment orders, which maintain minimum inventory levels.

Supply Network Planning is a midterm planning practice. Typical planning horizons cover several weeks or months.

The practice of Perfect Pick Put-Away entails ensuring that items are in the correct quantity, physical location, and condition so that they can be picked accurately when they are ordered.

Here are some best practices for ensuring Perfect Pick Put-Away:

- Check that the items are received from production in the correct quantity and in a saleable condition.

- If necessary, check that the relevant quality management steps have been completed.

- Ensure that the relevant supporting documentation, such as a certificate of analysis, is available.

- Check that the items have been stored in the correct quantity and in the correct storage location or warehouse bin and that all relevant warehouse postings have been confirmed.

best_practice_name: Days of Supply-Based Material Requirements Planning (MRP) Proposal Management
best_practice_definition:
Days of Supply-Based Material Requirements Planning (MRP) Proposal Management is the practice of reviewing and maintaining material requirements planning proposals by days of supply. It entails understanding demand and the corresponding Make proposals and then monitoring the exceptions. Management by exception, especially when working with production proposals for a select number of stock-keeping units in a vast product range, is key to an efficient planning process.

Typical process steps for this practice include the following:

- Evaluate planned orders for production based on output from MRP, with reference to the oldest demand.

- Validate MRP proposals matching demand so that business rules are satisfied.

- Reschedule where necessary and possible.

- Adjust proposal quantities and dates according to business intelligence from sales and operations planning and other resources.

Work Center Load Evaluation is the practice of identifying bottlenecks in operations and then evaluating the planned loads on these work centers, including work center loading over the optimal time horizon(s), pooled capacities, and work center hierarchies. Record all relevant information for input into balancing processes. Also, consider shift pattern efficiencies, breakdowns, and maintenance shutdowns in the evaluation and planning. Record all relevant information for input into balancing processes.

Balance and Firm within Horizon is the practice of balancing and firming up production activities and available resources in order to best satisfy demand while managing various resources, materials, and other constraints.

Here are some important tips for this practice:

- Manually or automatically schedule material requirements planning (MRP) proposals by date and quantity to optimize the given work center - loads within the agreed firm horizon.

- Delete any proposals that cannot be satisfied within the firm horizon. These proposals can be regenerated outside the firm horizon after the next MRP run.

- Record specific extraordinary items for input into the sales and operations planning plan.

Comments: The assumption is that run times and available capacity are correct.

The Production Plan is the agreed-upon plan that comes from the production planning (sales and operations planning) process—specifically, the overall level of manufacturing output planned to be produced, usually stated as a monthly rate for each product family (group of products, items, options, features, and so on). Various units of measurement (e.g., units, tonnage, standard hours, number of workers) can be used to express the plan. Represents management’s authorization for the master scheduler to convert it into a more detailed plan—that is, the master production schedule: aka: sales and operations planning, sales plan.

Characteristics-Based Forecasting (CBF) is a powerful tool that enables organizations to forecast demand on both the product and the characteristics levels. Configurable products have characteristics, which can take several values. This value assignment is called configuration of a product variant. Although there may be many possible hypothetical combinations, not all of them will be used because some will yield undesirable product variants or products that cannot be produced. In CBF, organizations can produce demand plans for combinations of characteristic values or for individual values. In general, organizations tend to focus on demand for the values that are most relevant to their business plans.

best_practice_name: Bill of Material (BOM) Audit and Control
best_practice_definition: Bill of Material (BOM) Audit and Control is the process that assesses the degree to which a list of specified items conforms to administrative specifications and with correct quantities.

Logistics and Warehouse Planning is the practice of considering the following key points during the Plan process rather than the Transform process: distribution channels, locations, modes of transportation, regulations, required paperwork, duties and taxes, and warehouse capacity.

The Logistics and Warehouse Planning process is a subset of the overall supply chain planning process, which also includes material requirements planning and distribution requirements planning. The inputs to Warehouse and Logistics Planning flow from the overall supply chain plan.
Supplier Appraisal is the practice of identifying suitable suppliers who can meet the planned requirements.

Mobile Access of Information in the supply chain means that information about status, metrics, supply, and demand are available through internet-enabled mobile devices. This requires the integration of the heterogeneous hardware and software components that form the supply chain. The hardware can include smartphones, tablets, laptops, and other mobile and handheld devices. The software includes enterprise resources planning software, various databases, and middleware network programs and protocols.

A Data Warehouse is a repository of data that has been specially prepared to support decision-making applications. Syn: decision-support data.

Business Intelligence is the information collected by an organization on customers, competitors, products or services, and processes.

Business intelligence provides organizational data in such a way that the organizational knowledge filters can easily associate with this data and turn it into information for the organization. Persons involved in business intelligence processes may use application software and other technologies to gather, store, analyze, and provide access to data and present that data in a simple, useful manner. The software aids in business performance management and aims to help consumers make better business decisions by offering them accurate, current, and relevant information. Some businesses use data warehouses because they are a logical collection of information gathered from various operational databases for the purpose of creating business intelligence.

Strategic Sourcing is a comprehensive approach for locating and sourcing key material suppliers, which often includes the business process of analyzing total-spend-for-material spend categories. Includes a focus on the development of long-term relationships with trading partners who can help the purchaser meet profitability and customer satisfaction goals. From an information technology applications perspective, includes automation of requests for quote (RFQ), requests for proposal (RFP), electronic auctioning (e-auction or reverse auction), and contract management processes.

The Purchasing and Procurement Strategy is the purchasing plan for categories (direct, indirect, strategic), families of items (commodities), and long-term risk mitigation to improve supply chain resilience. Includes the plan to manage the supplier base and solve problems.

Pick List Generation is the process of creating a sequential list of all components and materials required to fulfill a specific production, sales, or interplant order, also known as a pick list.

A pick list often specifies the location of each component or material so that warehouse personnel can efficiently locate the items and assemble material for orders. Items typically are ordered by warehouse location so that the picker, which can be a human, robot, drone, or another piece of automated equipment, can go through the warehouse and easily retrieve items for an order. This also sometimes enables warehouse personnel to consolidate picks for more than one order. Items typically are picked into transport bins for each order, packed, and then scheduled for shipment.

A pick list can be as simple as a manually created spreadsheet or a report automatically generated by a warehouse management system.

Customer Data Line of Responsibility is the practice of clearly assigning ownership and accountability for customer data and then periodically reviewing the data quality and accuracy in order to continuously improve the condition of the data and conduct root cause corrective action for any issues or errors. As part of the review, data quality accuracy and other metrics should be tracked to assess performance trends.

Facility Master Planning is a group of business processes that includes the following activities: demand management (which includes forecasting and order servicing); production and resource planning; and master scheduling (which includes the master schedule and the rough-cut capacity plan).

Task Management is a practice used to determine the resources and sequence of tasks for complex delivery processes, including aggregation and staging of products for shipment. Task Management allows the company to forecast manpower, skill set and capital equipment need to comply with committed shipment and delivery dates.

Effective Task Management includes managing all aspects of a task, including its status, priority, time, human and financial resources, recurrences, and notifications.
Predictive Maintenance is a type of preventive maintenance based on nondestructive testing and statistical analysis, used to predict when required maintenance should be scheduled.

Order Management involves the planning, directing, monitoring, and controlling of the processes related to customer orders, manufacturing orders, and purchase orders. Regarding customer orders, order management includes order promising, order entry, order pick, pack and ship, billing, and reconciliation of the customer account. Regarding manufacturing orders, order management includes order release, routing, manufacture, monitoring, and receipt into stores or finished goods inventories. Regarding purchasing orders, order management includes order placement, monitoring, receiving, acceptance, and payment of a supplier.

Return Policy Conformance Integration is the practice of implementing standard procedures and enabling technology to ensure conformance to return policies. Automated policies and supporting processes collect and share important failure and status data with the groups responsible for repair and overhaul, disposal, product life cycle management, component part procurement, and production planning and scheduling.

Carcass Prepositioning is the practice of making disposition decisions for reparable parts, cores, and carcasses early in the return material authorization process. Instructions for those decisions must be included in the authorization provided to the customers responsible for shipping and the internal stakeholders responsible for receiving. Routing decisions also should be included in those instructions. When long lead time, high-demand, or prioritization criteria are applied, items are automatically inducted into the maintenance, repair, and operations process, routing the items to a storage location or disposal.

best_practice_name: Product Development, Engineering and Disposition Collaboration
best_practice_definition: Product development and engineering groups should be in constant contact and communication with the disposition authority. Product development and engineering teams need to be aware of disposition decisions so that these groups can update technical documentation, the configuration management system, and product specifications as needed.

best_practice_name: Electronic Technical Orders and Product Specifications
best_practice_definition:
Electronic Technical Orders and Product Specifications is the practice of using digital methodologies and products to develop technical data for the engineering design, development, and manufacturing of products. This includes the utilization of portable maintenance aids, integrated electronic technical manuals, job performance aids, and other forms of Electronic Technical Orders and Product Specifications to aid in identifying product condition. These tools should tie into the product life cycle management and configuration management systems to ensure that any changes to product or system specifications are utilized in evaluating the product condition.

Such digital methodologies have demonstrated cost savings, process improvements, and increased interoperability.

In Return Shipping Consolidation, authorized returns are routed to the central consolidation hubs or facilities, such as a third-party logistics provider, closest to the customer. The gatekeeping function routes products to the right locations, eliminating the need for sorting at the hub. Consolidated shipments of items that need repair or disposal are transferred to the appropriate location in larger volumes, thus reducing handling, overall processing time, and associated processing and transportation costs.
A Cross-Functional Team is a set of individuals from various departments assigned a specific task, such as implementing new computer software.

Order Quotation System is the practice of receiving, managing, and responding to requests for quotations (RFQs) from customers. The functional group responsible for accepting and managing the RFQs should have the information, systems, and abilities to:

- provide immediate pricing and associated pricing discounts for various quantity breaks (for both similar items and mixed orders, if applicable)

- provide lead-time estimates for all items and order lines, including fulfillment estimates according to the original customer requirements as well as adjusted and negotiated dates, if applicable

- identify and provide alternative quotations based on additional configurations that would provide similar performance at a lower cost

- convert initial or subsequent quotations directly into firm orders.

Typically, an organization's customer service group would manage this practice. However, in the event that a functional group other than the customer service or order management group, such as the commercial pricing group, is responsible for this process element, then the ability to seamlessly move customer quotes between internal functions also is a critical element of this practice.

A Transportation Management System (TMS) is a computer application system designed to manage transportation operations. Typically offer modules focused on specific functions, such as intermodal transportation, import/export management, fleet service management, and load planning and optimization.

Expedited Logistics is the process of accelerating or chasing production, transportation, or purchase orders that are needed in less than the normal lead time; to take extraordinary action because of an increase in relative priority, aka stockchase.

To Embed Specialized Services is the practice of adding additional capability, processes, and expertise on-site by contracting with a third party. By leveraging their existing networks and assets and embedding third-party services, including specialized packaging, product completion, pack out, and other services, into their manufacturing and distribution operations, organizations can add significant capabilities to their supply chains without significant supply chain redesign and reengineering.

Transportation Management Outsourcing is the process of outsourcing the requirements for the execution of planning, scheduling, and budgeting of transportation assets, services, and related systems of the shipping process through delivery.

best_practice_name: Generation of Dynamic Bills of Materials (BOMs)
best_practice_definition: The Generation of Dynamic BOMs uses an information technology application to dynamically create BOMs based on customer order requirements and specifications as well as product rules. This can be especially useful in Make-to-Order environments so that a company can substitute different raw material types on the fly and create new but similar BOMs for a one-off production requirement.
3-D Printing and Rapid Prototyping is the process of layering materials to make products and components using computer data, aka additive manufacturing.

Digital Packaging on Demand can be used to create custom product packaging unique to the customer and the product requirements. The packaging is digitally printed and cut to a per-order design. This process enables packaging companies to create unique physical and graphic designs in small quantities. The ability to produce short-run on-demand packaging increases efficiency and reduces inventory management, storage and waste.

Vendor-Managed Inventory (VMI) is a means of optimizing supply chain performance in which the supplier has access to the customer’s inventory data and is responsible for maintaining the inventory level required by the customer. Accomplished by a process in which resupply is performed by the vendor through regularly scheduled reviews of the on-site inventory. The on-site inventory is counted, damaged or outdated goods are removed, and the inventory is restocked to predefined levels. The vendor obtains a receipt for the restocked inventory and accordingly invoices the customer; aka: continuous replenishment.

Return Load Optimization is the practice of combining customer deliveries with pickups for returned items to optimize transportation. In the technology industry, it is common to combine service delivery with the pickup or replacement of defective products at the customer site.
Return Shipment Insurance is the practice of buying insurance for high-value excess inventory return shipments.

best_practice_name: Automated Identification and Disposition of Overshipments
best_practice_definition: Automated supply chain management systems allow for the verification and identification of overshipped products at the time of receipt. Such systems usually automatically compare the received items with the purchase order tolerances. The information about the quantity of excess items can be used to take action based on policies and business rules related to the return process. Depending on company policies and the agreement between the parties involved, overshipped products can be shipped back immediately or sent to a requested return location to continue with the next step in the process.

Collaboration between supply chain partners can be facilitated using a Supply Chain Control Tower. This allows the supplier to see requirements and inventory levels at the customer’s site, highlighting any potential excess inventory. Similarly, the customer can easily identify supply and demand variations and take the necessary actions to return excess inventory, if needed.

Automated Alerts for Material Management is the practice of using web-based or email alerts containing enterprise resources planning insights to inform key supply chain partners about inventory levels and projected demand for key materials, as well as supply-demand imbalances. Predetermined thresholds, which typically are analyzed in terms of days of supply, need to be identified and agreed upon. Automated alerts can then notify decision-makers when inventory reaches upper and lower thresholds until action is taken to correct the supply-demand imbalance.

Return Cost Recovery is the practice of recovering the cost of materials and the incremental costs of returning the item to the supplier of the failing component and repairing the item. When a defective product is returned by a customer, an analysis to identify the source of the problem usually takes place. If the defect is determined to be related to a component purchased from a vendor, the process of recovering part or all of the cost from the vendor is typically called Return Cost Recovery. Further collaboration with the vendor to prevent similar issues in the future, or to improve quality, can also be considered.

best_practice_name: Return Policy Included with Shipping Document
best_practice_definition: Return Policy Included with Shipping Document - In order to better facilitate the return process and provide additional information about agreed-upon return policies, it is common practice to include the return policy with the shipping documentation. This clearly identifies terms and conditions and explains what kind of action should be taken in case of a return.

The Identification of Obsolete Capital Assets is the process of identifying physical assets that are held by an organization for its production potential and that are no longer usable or have zero value.

A Request for Information (RFI) is an inquiry to a potential supplier about that supplier’s product or service for potential use in the business. The inquiry can provide certain business requirements or be of a more general exploratory nature, aka request for proposal (RFP).
A Request for Quote (RFQ) is a document used to solicit vendor responses when a product has been selected and price quotations are needed from several vendors.

Total Preventive Maintenance Programs encompass continuing efforts to adapt, modify, and refine equipment to increase flexibility, reduce material handling, and promote continuous flows. It is operator-oriented maintenance with the involvement of all qualified employees in all maintenance activities, aka total preventive maintenance.

Supplier Evaluation is the practice of evaluating a new or existing supplier. A thorough supplier evaluation process will consider pricing, technical quality, supplier structure and sustainability, capability and capacity, fit with the purchasing company, level of service, performance history, location, and acceptable contract terms and conditions. It is prudent to be as objective as possible in the evaluation. Weighting can be given to certain evaluation criteria, such as price, quality, performance, or location, based on their importance to the purchaser.

An evaluation committee should jointly agree on the overall evaluation score. Members of the committee should include key stakeholders, purchasers, and individuals who may not have a direct interest in the outcome but who are able to ask probing questions and challenge the norm.

This task should not be confused with evaluation of supplier materials.

The Return Authorization process in which the last known holder or the designated return center receives a return authorization request from a customer determines if the item can be accepted, and communicates the decision to the customer. Requests from the customer can be made for reasons of defect, excess, recall, etc. Accepting the request includes negotiating the conditions of the return with the customer, including authorizing replacement or credit. Rejecting the request includes providing a reason for the rejection to the customer.
Outsourcing the supply chain dedicated to the reverse flow of products and materials for the purpose of returns, repair, remanufacture, and/or recycling.
Carcass Disassembly refers to the disassembling of a non-serviceable item obtained from a customer that is intended for use in remanufacturing.

Theory of Constraints (TOC) is a holistic management philosophy developed by Dr. Eliyahu M. Goldratt, based on the principle that complex systems exhibit inherent simplicity. Even a very complex system comprising thousands of people and pieces of equipment can have, at any given time, only a very, very small number of variables—perhaps only one, known as a constraint— that actually limit the ability to generate more of the system’s goal.

Pre-issued Return Authorization is the practice in which a return authorization number is issued at the time of ordering or shipment of the goods to the customer.
