The proactive issuance of a return authorization number reduces the time, cost, and possible errors associated with the process to receive and validate a return authorization request and issuing the authorization. This practice also requires the policy that an item cannot be returned without a return authorization number.

Preventive Returns is the practice of issuing notices to consumers and customers requesting the return of goods or materials due to possible product defects or damage. This includes notifying distributors, intermediaries or channel partners that may hold these goods for resale purposes. The purpose of preventive returns is to protect the brand, reduce operational disruptions for customers, avoid injuries to customers or consumers, and reduce associated costs.

Examples of preventive returns include recalls in the automotive, electronics, and food industries.

Purchase Order Management is the management of a purchaser’s authorization used to formalize a purchase transaction with a supplier. A purchase order, when given to a supplier, should contain statements of the name, part number, quantity, description, and price of the goods or services ordered; agreed-to terms as to payment, discounts, date of performance, and transportation; and all other agreements pertinent to the purchase and its execution by the supplier.

Supplier Collaboration is the practice of issuing a 12-month rolling picture of demand to the supplier. The schedule usually includes a fixed window of time in which no changes should be made, a flexible window where it is acceptable to increase or decrease quantities or adjust delivery times, and a forecast window that gives the supplier an idea of future plans. The schedules are reviewed regularly, often on a monthly basis. This collaboration may enable suppliers to provide a higher level of service at a lower cost.

In situations where Supplier Collaboration is being used, there usually is a formal contract between the supplier and the customer that includes the agreed-upon prices, specifications, and delivery volumes. With this aspect handled, the strategic purchasing team can focus on the commercial points, and the operational purchaser can focus on managing the order requirements and demands of production. These are two very different skill sets, but they are equally important here.

The expectation is that lead times become reduced as suppliers can plan resources with fewer surprises. This practice often is used in industries that have regular purchases of products. It is especially beneficial to industries that must manage variation and changes.

Cross-Docking is the concept of packing products on incoming shipments so they can be easily sorted at intermediate warehouses or for outgoing shipments based on the final destination. The items are carried from the incoming vehicle docking point to the outgoing vehicle docking point without being stored in inventory at the warehouse. Cross-docking reduces inventory investment and storage space requirements. aka direct loading.

Receiving Goods Inspection is the practice of inspecting goods upon receipt for any delivery discrepancies such as damage, incorrect quantity compared with a purchase order or delivery paperwork, and incomplete or incorrect paperwork. In some cases, receiving personnel should test samples of some materials to ensure accuracy. If any check shows a discrepancy, the goods may be quarantined or rejected following the returns process. The returns process will need to ensure that the vendor provides credit for goods returned.
3-Way Delivery Verification is the practice of comparing the information on purchase orders, receipts, and invoices to ensure that the correct items were received and invoiced.

best_practice_name: Supply Chain Risk Management (SCRM) Strategy Implementation and Analysis
best_practice_definition: The Supply Chain Risk Management (SCRM) Strategy Implementation and Analysis is the strategic implementation of the identification, assessment, and prioritization of risks followed by coordinated and economical application of resources to minimize, monitor, and control the probability and/or impact of unfortunate events or to maximize the realization of opportunities.

The Supply Chain Risk Register is a report that has summary information on qualitative risk analysis, quantitative risk analysis, and risk response planning. This register contains all identified risks and associated details.

A risk register captures all of the risk exposure for a supply chain once the risks are identified and assessed in terms of impact and probability of occurrence. While developing this register, organizations often name major risk groups, including operational, technical, financial, legal, brand, environmental, and safety and health risks. Then they identify specific supply chain risks within the groups and capture the impact of these specific risks on their respective key risk groups.

A risk matrix is then developed by plotting the probability of occurrence on one axis and impact on the other. For each supply chain risk identified, risk management professionals should plot it on the matrix. This will help the risk management team arrive at a risk rating for each risk and accurately prioritize the risk.

Real-Time Package Tracking is the practice of using technology to track the movement and location of packages in real time. A radio frequency identification tag or machine-to-machine antenna is attached to the package or asset, which allows the owner, seller, or buyer to track the item via GPS, cellular phone, or other networks.

Tracking information also can include current trajectory, travel history, vehicle speed, package temperature, and level of light exposure. Alerts may be established to notify customers or owners of various changes to package conditions, including high or low temperatures, as well as when a package has been picked up, is in transit, or has been successfully delivered.

Trackers can be placed in each package, sporadically throughout a related shipment, or within courier satchels and vehicles. Self-powered GPS trackers are useful. When GPS signals are unavailable, tracking devices should automatically default to a cellular network and relay their positions through the closest cell tower.

Automated Data Capture (ADC) is the use of technologies that collects data about objects and then sends the data to a computer without human intervention. Examples include radio frequency wireless devices and terminals, bar code scanners, and smart cards.

Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) is a system that uses electronic tags to store data about items. Accessing or retrieving this data is accomplished through a specific radio frequency and does not require close proximity or line-of-sight access, aka active tag, passive tag, or semi-passive tag.

Standard Operating Procedures is the practice of creating, using, and following a written document or instruction guide that details all of the steps and activities of a process or procedure. A standard operating procedure (SOP) provides employees with a reference for completing common business practices, activities, or tasks. New employees use an SOP to answer their questions without having to interrupt supervisors to ask how an operation is performed.
Well-documented SOPs help ensure consistency in process execution and provide an effective tool for documenting process steps and their sequence, business rules, best practices, and exception handling, as well as who is responsible for each step.

The international quality standard ISO 9001 essentially requires the determination and documentation of processes used in any manufacturing process that could affect the quality of the product. Standard Operating Procedures can support this.

Collaborative Planning, Forecasting, and Replenishment (CPFR) is a collaborative process whereby supply chain trading partners can jointly plan key supply chain activities from production and delivery of raw materials to production and delivery of final products to end customers. Collaboration encompasses business planning, sales forecasting, and all operations required to replenish raw materials and finished goods. 2) A process philosophy for facilitating collaborative communications. CPFR is considered a standard and is endorsed by the Voluntary Interindustry Commerce Standards, aka collaborative planning.

Just-in-Time (JIT) Production is a philosophy of manufacturing based on the planned elimination of all waste and on continuous improvement of productivity. It encompasses the successful execution of all manufacturing activities required to produce a final product, from design engineering to delivery, and includes all stages of conversion from raw material onward. The primary elements of just in time are to have only the required inventory when needed; to improve quality to zero defects; to reduce lead times by reducing setup times, queue lengths, and lot sizes; to incrementally revise the operations themselves, and to accomplish these activities at minimum cost. In the broad sense, it applies to all forms of manufacturing—job shop, process, and repetitive—and to many service industries as well, aka short-cycle manufacturing, stockless production, zero inventories.

A goods receipt from a production environment where products can be and usually are finished before receipt of a customer order. Customer orders are typically filled from existing stocks, and production orders are used to replenish those stocks, aka produce-to-stock, assemble-to-order, make-to-order.

Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) is the paperless (electronic) exchange of trading documents, such as purchase orders, shipment authorizations, advanced shipment notices, and invoices, using standardized document formats.

Lean is a philosophy of production that emphasizes the minimization of the amount of all the resources (including time) used in the various activities of the enterprise. It involves identifying and eliminating non-value-adding activities in design, production, supply chain management, and dealing with customers. Lean producers employ teams of multiskilled workers at all levels of the organization and use highly flexible, increasingly automated machines to produce volumes of products in potentially enormous variety. Lean production contains a set of principles and practices to reduce cost through the relentless removal of waste and through the simplification of all manufacturing and support processes, aka lean, lean manufacturing.

Spend Analysis is a purchasing activity in which a firm explores its spending patterns to identify opportunities to reduce costs or improve quality. Part of value analysis as well as cost-benefit analysis.

Long-Term Supplier Agreement or Partnership is the practice of using long-term agreements to replace multiple purchase orders for repetitive or recurring orders. More complex agreements involve a longer-term strategic partnership that includes the sharing of knowledge as well as supplier involvement in early product development.

These agreements can vary from very informal for very formal, such as those bound by strict legal contracts. In addition, the agreements can be between a buyer and a simple supplier of a commodity or between a buyer and a partner in the value chain.

The practice aims at achieving total quality management across the value chain.

Supply Base Rationalization is the practice of analyzing the number of suppliers an organization uses to determine if it is the optimum number. One of the measures of purchasing performance is average purchasing volume per supplier. The buying company needs to strike a balance between the number of suppliers for a material or product and the buying company’s negotiating power. Increasing the number of suppliers used can enhance competition and drive down prices. At the same time, using too many suppliers could also have negative effects. For example, each supplier may provide a smaller amount of items or materials, which could exempt the buyer from receiving quantity-based discounts. In addition, managing multiple suppliers creates more work for purchasing managers.

A spend analysis is a very good starting point for creating a guideline for the optimum number of suppliers.

Consignment Inventory Management is a technique to manage inventories, generally of finished goods, that are in the possession of customers, dealers, agents, brokers, etc., but remain the property of the manufacturer by agreement with those in possession, aka consignment inventory, vendor-owned inventory, consignment.

best_practice_name: Convergence of SCOR with Lean and Six Sigma
best_practice_definition: Lean Six Sigma is a methodology that combines the improvement concepts of lean and six sigma. It uses the seven wastes of lean and the DMAIC process from six sigma, and awards recognition of competence through judo-style belts. Leveraging SCOR as part of the method helps organizations develop larger, more impactful improvement portfolios.

Document Management System is the practice of using of a computer system or set of programs to track and store electronic documents or images of paper documents. Document management systems generally are capable of keeping track of different versions created by different users for the purposes of version control and tracking changes. Document management systems are considered a component of enterprise content management systems and are related to digital asset management, document imaging, workflow systems and records management systems.

Document Management System eliminates the need for managing paper versions of documents as well as the challenges of archiving and document retention. In addition, document management systems allow multiple people to access the documents, sometimes at the same time, which is not typically possible with paper documents.

Electronic Returns Tracking is the practice of using electronic systems to track the locations of returns within the supply chain. This practice enables shorter turn-around times for returns, repairs and replacements. Visibility of in-transit items also can help recipients identify and plan for shipping delays.

This practice can involve different types of technology, including bar coding and radio frequency identification. Regardless of the type of technology used, an information technology system must be set up to track item locations as they are scanned and display this information to supply chain analysts.

More sophisticated systems can be set up to do automated analysis of information to immediately identify potential issues. An example may be reviewing transfer cycle times to see if they fall within a certain time limit. If the metric falls outside the desired range, the system could notify a supply chain analyst to resolve the issue. Setting up business rules and notifications within a tracking system helps to automate the return process and reduce required manpower.

Rotable Spares Pool is the use of an inventory of serviceable parts that can replace a customer’s broken part to help minimize customer downtime. This is especially useful for items that tend to have long lead times.

However, a challenge with this strategy is ensuring that the parts in the rotable spares pool are a form, fit and function replacement for any items that a customer could bring in for exchange. There also is a risk that parts in the rotable spares pool could become obsolete, which yields high costs for the company. Therefore, this practice is best used for high-demand items with long lead times, such as structural items that frequently break and need repair.

Beyond Economic Repair (BER) Management is the practice of assessing items as they are removed for Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO) to determine whether repairing the items would cost more than buying replacements. Determining this before shipping an item for repair can reduce transportation costs. Any salvageable components should be taken off an item before scrapping it, so that these components can be used as additional repair parts.

The identification process may require test equipment and other assessment tools or personnel at the site where the BER assessment is being made. Depots are a likely location for this practice to take place because of the availability of tools and personnel.

best_practice_name: Mixed Mode or Reverse Material Issue
best_practice_definition:
Mixed Mode or Reverse Material Issue is a practice that helps accurately track raw material levels before and after-production. It is most useful on production lines where the amount of raw material needed tends to vary based on different parameters.

This defers from the back flush concept, in which a system automatically issues the same amount of raw material each time a product is manufactured. For example, assume that a widget requires two units of raw material. Once one widget is manufactured, two more units of raw material are released so that the next widget can be made. The drawback of this system is that there is no real-time visibility of the raw materials in the whole process. The accuracy of the inventory count also is dependent on the theoretical assumption that two units of raw material are required to make one widget.

However, in Mixed Mode or Reverse Material Issue, an automated system or human operator checks the amount of leftover raw material after each item is produced and then returns the leftover raw material to inventory. So, for example, if only 1.8 units of raw material are required to make a widget, the leftover 0.2 units could be returned to inventory, rather than scrapped or lost in the process. Similarly, if 2.2 units are needed, then the operator or automated system can adjust the raw materials inventory record to note that 0.2 fewer units are available for future production. The advantage of this system is that there is an accurate count of the amount of raw material in inventory at any given time.
Production Scheduling Optimization Using Technology is a process of developing the production schedule using smart technologies that employ advanced algorithms, machine learning, and AI.
Supply Chain Risk Monitoring is the practice of establishing a formal process to continuously monitor the changes in probability or impact of risk events.

Supply Chain Risk Assessment provides management with an understanding of where the greatest risks may exist. This helps company leaders prioritize resources for risk mitigation and management. Performing such assessments will involve clarifying the nature of a risk, understanding conditions that may lead to the event, knowing how frequently such events have happened or can be expected to happen, and the potential impact of such events. The team can then prioritize addressing the risks. Risk assessment typically is made up of two measures: probability and impact:

Probability measures the likelihood that a supply chain–interrupting event will occur. In formal probability, a probability of 0 means the event will never occur, and a probability of 1 means the event will surely occur. The exact probability may be difficult to determine unless historical data exist that can be used to find the frequency of the risk event. Alternatively, an organization can use a subjective probability, or degree of belief, based on the opinions of experts. A time horizon is necessary to define the probability in a useful way, for example, the likelihood that an event will occur in the next year or in the next 50 years.

Impact measures the consequences of risk event on the organization. It can be measured directly, for example, in terms of monetary impact, or on a scale, for example on a scale of zero to one with zero being very little negative consequence, 0.5 being a medium amount of consequence, and one being a very severe consequence. Methods for measuring impact include what-if simulations, financial models and the opinions of teams of experts. Impact may also be measured in terms of other SCOR metrics besides financials.
Additive Manufacturing is the process of layering materials to make products and components using computer data, aka additive manufacturing See: BP.120 3D Printing and Rapid Prototyping.

A Blockchain is a continuously growing list of records, called blocks, are linked, and secured using cryptography. Each block typically contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, a timestamp, and transaction data. The data in any given block cannot be altered retroactively without the alteration of all subsequent blocks, inherently making it resistant to modification, aka cryptocurrency.
Demand-Driven Material Requirements Planning (DDMRP) is a method for planning material needs that enables a company to build more closely to actual market requirements.

Demand-Driven Sales and Operations Planning (DDS&OP) is a bidirectional integration point in a demand-driven adaptive system between the strategic (annual, quarterly, and monthly) and tactical (hourly, daily, and weekly) relevant ranges of decision-making. DDS&OP sets the key parameters of a demand-driven operating model based on business strategy, market intelligence, and key business objectives, including strategic information and requirements. DDS&OP also projects model performance based on the strategic information and requirements and various model settings. In addition, DDS&OP uses variance analysis based on past model performance in terms of reliability, stability, and velocity to adapt the key parameters of a demand-driven operating model and even recommend strategic alterations to the model and project their respective impacts on the business.

A Digital Supply Chain encompasses the process of delivering digital media, such as music or video files, by electronic means from the point of origin at the content provider to the destination with the consumer. Similar to how a physical item must go through a supply chain process in order to mature from components to a consumable product, digital media must pass through various stages in processing before it can be enjoyed by a consumer via a smartphone, tablet, computer, television or another device.

A broader definition of the term digital supply chain is the use of digital technology and content to improve supply chain performance. Part of this refined definition recognizes that traditional supply chains configured to distribute physical goods or services can be enhanced via technology — such as computers and other connected devices, the internet of things, and related sensors — and digital content. For example, real-time monitoring of equipment can allow companies to proactively schedule maintenance or replace parts. Similarly, real-time inventory tracking can enable proactive reordering of materials, components, or products. Companies also can provide enhanced user support for a physical item through digital content, such as videos demonstrating how to use or troubleshoot a product. Digital supply chains are enabled by the internet of things, cloud-based computing, big data, and advanced analytics, among other technologies.

The Internet of Things (IOT) is an environment in which objects, animals, or people are provided with unique identifiers and the ability to transfer data over a network without requiring human-to-human or human-to-computer interaction. This allows objects to be sensed and controlled remotely across existing network infrastructure, creating opportunities for more direct integration between the physical world and computer-based systems.

Integrated Business Planning (IBP) is a business process and capability that seeks to maximize company profitability by creating an enterprise-wide operating plan. The process drives decision-making across all aspects of the business by balancing customer demand, supply, and company resources. The integrated business plan is generated at the level of detail needed for all participating business functions to execute the activities required to achieve the plan. This is typically at an aggregate planning level with the ability to disaggregate to a more detailed level.

IBP is a mid-term planning process that focuses on month two and beyond, extending out past the fiscal year typically to 18 months. (Timeframes vary depending on the industry sector.) The goal of the IBP process is to develop consensus on a single business plan that aligns with the strategy, tactics, and execution plans; organization and functional accountabilities; and any risk management plans.

The IBP process is owned by the executive or senior management team and is cross-functional in nature. Distinct to IBP is the appropriate integration, involvement, and commitment of functions or areas such as product management, finance, new product introduction, product marketing, engineering, service and support, sales, demand planning and forecasting, operations and manufacturing, and sourcing and procurement. An IBP process typically builds upon the foundation of an established Sales and Operations Planning (S&OP) (BP.021) process with continuous review meetings in each functional area.

IBP is unique from S&OP because it also includes other advanced practices, including Scenario Planning (BP.184) and Supply Chain Risk Management (SCRM) (BP.001)
Scenario Planning is a planning process that identifies critical events before they occur and uses this knowledge to determine effective alternatives.

The Cost of Quality Measurement represents the overall costs associated with prevention activities and the improvement of quality throughout the firm before, during, and after the production of a product. These costs fall into four recognized categories: internal failure costs, external failure costs, appraisal costs, and prevention costs. Internal failure costs relate to problems before the product reaches the customer. These usually include rework, scrap, downgrades, reinspection, retest, and process losses. External failure costs relate to problems found after the product reaches the customer. These usually include such costs as warranty and returns. Appraisal costs are associated with the formal evaluation and audit of quality in the firm. Typical costs include inspection, quality audits, testing, calibration, and checking time. Prevention costs are those caused by improvement activities that focus on reducing failure and appraisal costs. Typical costs include education, quality training, and supplier certification, aka cost of poor quality.

Supply Chain Finance is a technology-based set of processes that link the buyer, seller, and financing institution to lower financing costs and improved business efficiency. Specifically, Supply Chain Finance provides short-term credit to the buyer, and the seller then optimizes that working capital. Technology is used to automate transactions and track invoice approval and the settlement process.

The purpose of Supply Chain Financing is to increase value; mitigate risk; and improve financial performance through collaborative relationships that plan, steer, control, and manage the supply and demand of financial resources in the supply network.

Supply Chain Finance has relevance and impact across individual businesses (micro level), total supply chains (meso level), and the national and global economy (macro level).

best_practice_name: Supply Chain Management Object Synchronization (3- or 4-Way Match)
best_practice_definition:
Supply Chain Management Object Synchronization (3- or 4-Way Match) provides the ability to follow an object through its entire life cycle across a supply chain is a foundational element in creating visibility and gaining supply chain control. The focuses of Supply Chain Management Object Synchronization are to create object synchronization from sales to cash and to enable systems integration and digitalization.

The method to describe the object linkages within the object synchronization is often referred to as a 3- or 4-Way Match.

Augmented Reality is the practice of integrating augmented reality (AR) technology into current processes to boost efficiency and automation. AR technology blurs the line between the physical and digital worlds. AR devices juxtapose holograms over a physical environment to provide additional information or guidance. Using AR in supply chain management can help make warehouse operations more efficient, speed up production, reduce machine downtime, minimize in-house costs and achieve shorter sales processes, thus boosting worker engagement and enhancing overall productivity.

Picking, for example, can be improved drastically by using AR. The operator can wear AR-enabled smart glasses to see information about the locations of items as well as instructions about what items and quantities to pick, all overlaid on his or her current field of vision. This allows employees to work in a heads-up manner, rather than having to constantly refer to pick sheets, which in turn enables faster cycle times to fulfill orders and a more efficient workforce without the expense of pick-to-light hardware.

Robotic Process Automation is a technology that replaces activities (processes) previously performed by humans with mechanical devices or data-oriented robots that can either be operated by humans or run by computers. Difficult to do, dangerous, or monotonous tasks are likely candidates for robots to perform.

Artificial Intelligence refers to computer programs (algorithms) that can learn and reason in a manner similar to humans. The problem is defined in terms of states and operators to generate a search space that is examined for the best solution. In contrast, conventional programming collects and processes data by algorithm or fixed step-by-step procedures.
Big Data Analytics is the process of collecting, storing, and processing massive amounts of data for the purpose of converting it into useful information.

Should Cost Modeling is an analytical approach that determines what a product should cost based on estimated costs for raw materials, labor, and production overhead as well as the profit margin. This practice essentially requires a customer to adopt the mindset of the supplier and estimate costs that typically are incurred by a supplier but are later rolled into an item price. Advanced, bottom-up should cost models provide insights into cost drivers, which are an important enabler for identifying cost reduction opportunities. These models can then be used during the bidding process in requests for proposals or requests for quotes, which typically results in better prices for low-spend items. Supplier-agreed cost models also can be used to enable longer-term supplier agreements, especially for product categories in which new products are frequently introduced during the contract duration.

Should Cost Modeling optimizes product and process design, which often are the drivers of cost; helps product development teams estimate the product cost at an early stage to achieve their targeted costs’ and provides the sourcing team with key information for judicious price negotiation. Should Cost Modeling also builds an understanding of the cost structure and enables companies to identify savings opportunities. In addition, it can help to identify the major cost drivers for a given item and compare them across supplier cost categories.

Predictive Analytics is a method of extracting information from existing data to determine patterns and predict future outcomes and trends. It does not predict with 100 percent accuracy, but it does predict unknown future events with a high level of reliability.

Predictive Analytics uses historical and current data as data sets to forecast future opportunities and risks. It also uses many different techniques like data mining, text analytics, statistics, modeling, artificial intelligence, and machine learning and applies them to structured and unstructured data sets to create predictive models that are then used to predict the likelihood of a particular event happening in the future. Predictive models capture relationships among many factors in a data set to assess the conditions and place a numerical value, called a score, on the likeliness of a particular future opportunity, risk, or event happening.

Predictive Analytics allows organizations to become more proactive and forward-looking and anticipate outcomes and behaviors based on data rather than hunches or assumptions. For example, retailers could use Predictive Analytics based on their own customer analytics to make more informed decisions about what types of products to stock. In addition, sensors on manufacturing machinery can collect data to help Predictive Analytics determine when maintenance and repair work should be done or when the machinery will stop working.

Digital Twin is the practice of making an exact virtual replica or model of a process, product, or service to digitally simulate, test, model and monitor the operations of a real-world object.

Although a digital twin can be created before the physical product is built, the virtual counterparts of physical assets typically are created using sensors on the physical objects. Data should be collected and synthesized from various sources, including physical data, manufacturing data, operational data, and data from other analytics software. This data, along with artificial intelligence and machine-learning algorithms, is integrated into a virtual model. As more data is collected and synthesized, the digital model becomes a better representation of the physical item, thus allowing operators to monitor and test equipment without being near or utilizing the item. In addition, real-time access to data can help companies better analyze situations and predict and identify problems before they escalate.

This practice is especially suited for the manufacturing and automobile industries. Digital twins can play a significant role in the way products are designed, manufactured, and maintained, which in turn increases the efficiency of and optimizes the process while also reducing throughput. In the automobile industry, an automaker can make a digital twin of a car to capture its behavioral and operational data and analyze its overall performance.

Smart Contracts involve the use of self-executing contracts to write the terms of an agreement between a buyer and a seller into lines of blockchain code and then use this technology to automatically ensure that the contract terms are met. If a new action, transaction, or other information is added to the blockchain, or decentralized digital ledger, of the agreement, the information will be rejected if it does not match the terms of the agreement already included in the blockchain, thus ensuring that all parties adhere to the contract.

This practice is especially useful in supporting trustworthy transactions between or among anonymous parties. Transactions made via smart contracts and blockchains are traceable, transparent, and irreversible.

The best way to describe a smart contract is to compare it to a vending machine. When making a purchase from a vending machine, the purchaser inserts payment and enters the number associated with the item he or she wants to buy. The vending machine then validates the request by checking the availability of the requested item and the amount of money inserted. If the validation is successful, the vending machine dispenses the item. Otherwise, it rejects the transaction and returns the money. There is no need for a middleman, such as a human cashier, in this transaction.

Many organizations across industries can benefit from Smart Contracts. For example, automated billing processes can reduce overbilling and prevent fraudulent billing. In turn, this also increases the speed of communication and transactions because the process is automated and transparent. Plus, because the contracts are self-monitoring, humans are not needed to oversee the contracts as meticulously as with regular contracts, thus freeing up personnel to handle other value-added tasks.

Advanced Data Visualization and Visibility is the practice of rendering complex data in a visual context so that people can understand the data better. Patterns and correlations that might go undetected in text-based data can be exposed and recognized when they are rendered visually using advanced data visualization techniques. To support a dynamic business environment with constantly flowing data streams, advanced data visualization tools also provide a more dynamic representation of data, displaying the information in sophisticated infographics, 3D geographic maps, heat maps, dials and gauges, multi-dimensional views, animations, and more. These images might include interactive capabilities as well, enabling users to manipulate them or mine data out of them to further analyze the situation.

A common Advanced Data Visualization and Visibility strategy is to generate a dashboard of automatically updating charts and graphics that help the organization track its performance over time and across different sectors.

Real-Time Location System is the use of real-time location systems (RTLS) to automatically identify and track the location of objects or people in real time. Tracked items or people are equipped with wireless RTLS tags that send wireless signals to fixed reference points to help the system determine the specific tag’s location. The system can be used to locate pallets of merchandise in a warehouse or find a specific bag in a retail store, for example. However, the locating capability typically is limited to the area equipped with receivers for the RTLS tag signals.

RTLS is different from GPS in that most RTLS utilize radio frequency communication and built-in electrical chips. In addition, RTLS is more interested in location than speed.

The retail industry can particularly benefit from this practice. For example, a clothing retailer can implant a chip into every hanger. Then, the system can track which items are still on the rack, have been picked up by a customer, have been brought to the fitting room, or have been returned to the rack. This can enable a store employee to help a customer quickly find a specific shirt in a specific size, for example, or receive customer feedback about how well an item tends to fit, based on how often the item is taken to the fitting room and then returned to the rack, without asking customers.

Autonomous Delivery is the practice of using robots that travel over land or through the air to deliver parcels. On-road autonomous vehicles can automatically collect packages, mail, or even food orders and deliver them to locations in urban areas. By comparison, drones and other air-based autonomous vehicles are better suited for suburban and rural deliveries. The advantages of this practice are that it frees up humans to handle other value-added tasks and that it helps organizations expand their same-day delivery capabilities, which could give them an advantage over competitors.

Stocktaking by Drones is the practice of using drones to count the stock or inventory in a given location. Drones are increasingly being used in warehouses to count stock by scanning bar codes or radio frequency identification tags or by using a computer vision system. The stock information then is relayed directly to the warehouse management system. Stocktaking drones may be fully autonomous, navigating through a warehouse using non-GPS systems such as lasers, 4G, or Wi-Fi for positioning, or they may be tethered to a forklift or autonomous warehouse vehicle and constantly monitor and record stock while the vehicle operates. Stocktaking drones also can operate outside of warehouses in open yards and storage areas using differential GPS and preprogrammed routes.

Stocktaking drones can operate 24/7 and provide high stock accuracy with minimum disruption to operations. In addition, stocktaking drones can increase safety by preventing humans from having to climb ladders to count stock that is stored in high locations.
Dynamic Inventory Management is the branch of business management concerned with planning and controlling inventories at all levels, horizons, and time fences.

A Quick Response (QR) Code is a unique, item-level code that can be added to a product. The QR code can carry product information and be used for inventory management, track and trace, authentication at the point of sale to help discern authentic items from counterfeit products, verifying warranties, and more.

Mobile Distribution Center is the practice of setting up movable storage tankers, mobile warehouses, or other mobile facilities that can quickly be installed in a building and positioned close to the customer to improve responsiveness and customer satisfaction. This practice may optimize a distribution network that deals with high demand and unexpected variability. The distribution designs of organizations that use this practice are not restricted by the location of the current infrastructure. Instead, the organizations can dynamically adjust their distribution locations to accommodate demand.

Machine Learning is the practice of using artificial intelligence that is capable of analysis, self-training, and observation to assist with planning and forecasting and also improve its own performance. Artificial intelligence systems can collect data, receive instructions, or observe examples and direct experiences and then identify patterns in the information. This analysis forms the basis of the technology’s knowledge, thus helping it to become smarter and more capable, and can help the system make decisions in the future. The primary aim is to allow the computers to learn automatically without human intervention or assistance and adjust actions accordingly.

Dynamic Routing provides real-time information management detailing the method of manufacture of a particular item. It includes the operations to be performed, their sequence, the various work centers involved, and the standards for setup and run. In some companies, the routing also includes information on tooling, operator skill levels, inspection operations, testing requirements, and so on, aka bill of operations, instruction sheet, manufacturing data sheet, operation chart, operation list, operation sheet, route sheet, routing sheet, bill of labor, bill of resources. In information systems, the process of defining the path a message will take from one computer to another computer.

Virtual Reality is the process of using interactive, computer-generated experiences(hardware and software) that take place within a simulated, apparently real environment for the purposes of training personnel or handling dangerous jobs remotely. Virtual reality (VR) technology mainly incorporates auditory and visual feedback, but some systems include haptic feedback as well. This helps with completing tasks or experiencing a realistic training simulation.

Current VR technology most commonly uses VR headsets or multi-projected environments, sometimes in combination with physical environments or props, to generate realistic images, sounds, and other sensations that simulate a user's physical presence in a virtual or imaginary environment.

A Multi-Enterprise Business Network (MEBN) is a commerce network or platform that facilitates the exchange of information or transactions among disparate parties within the scope of supply chain processes, including finance and settlement. A MEBN, in conjunction with multi-enterprise business applications, is sometimes referred to as a multi-enterprise supply chain business network (MESCBN). Regardless of the name, the best networks combine trading partner networks and advanced applications with intelligence to support all aspects of supply chain processes and functionality across the enterprise and with stakeholder groups and interested parties.

Crowdsourced Delivery is a fulfillment practice that leverages networks of local, non-professional couriers to deliver packages to customers' doors. Crowdsourced delivery attempts to skirt the bottlenecks of last-mile delivery by tasking someone local to both the package’s origin and customers' door to expedite fulfillment and elevate customer satisfaction.

Telematics is a method of monitoring cars, trucks, equipment, and other assets by using GPS technology and on-board diagnostics (OBD) to plot the asset’s movements on a computerized map. Also known as fleet tracking or GPS vehicle tracking, telematics is now an essential management tool for fleet management.

Fleet management is an essential operation for the efficient functioning of logistics operations from the first mile to the last mile, and it involves ensuring that the overall costs of transportation, fleet, and resource utilization, and regulatory compliance of a fleet are at their optimal. Effective fleet management through utilization of telematics, fleet tracking, messaging and alerting, arrival times predictions, dashboard provisioning, and carrier integration enables supply chain visibility and lets all relevant stakeholders know where shipments are at all times and in real-time.

A Smart Factory is an interconnected network of machines, communication mechanisms, and computing power, the smart factory is a cyber-physical system that uses advanced technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning to analyze data, drive automated processes, and learn as it goes. A smart factory provides real-time operational insight and intelligence across the supply chain to improve tactical and strategic operations and gain a competitive advantage. It is comprised of the following three attributes:

Connected: Enterprise is horizontally and vertically integrated to facilitate in real time the flow of intelligent data between people, processes, technology, and physical and virtual assets.
Real Time: Actual time during which a process or event occurs. Within the connected system, the input data and intelligent data are processed near real time, so it is available for immediate use.
Intelligent: Capable of analyzing in real-time states and/or actions in response to varying situations, requirements, and past experiences, and updating data accordingly.
Service Configuration Management is a formal procedure to identify and document the characteristics of a product, service, or project, control changes, and support an audit to verify conformance.
A Service Level Management document represents the terms of performance for organic support.

Service Change Management is the business process that coordinates and monitors all changes to the business processes, services and applications operated by the business, as well as to its internal equipment, resources, operating systems, and procedures. The change management discipline is carried out in a way that minimizes the risk of problems that will affect the operating environment and service delivery to the users.

Service Incident Management is the practice of managing the resolution of unplanned events that disrupt or can disrupt the service and involves recording, prioritizing, updating, and closing incidents.
Service Request Management is the practice of managing the fulfillment of service requests and includes recording, prioritizing, fulfilling, updating, and closing service requests.

Service Availability Management is the practice of ensuring that services meet the current and future availability needs of the business in a cost-effective and timely manner. Availability management defines, analyzed, plans, measures, and improves all aspects of the availability of services and ensures that all infrastructures, processes, tools, and roles are appropriate for the agreed service level targets.

Service Capacity Management is the function of establishing, measuring, monitoring, and adjusting limits or levels of capacity in order to execute all transformation activities (i.e., the service plan, production plan, master production schedule, material requirements plan, and dispatch list). Capacity management is executed at four levels: resource requirements planning, rough-cut capacity planning, capacity requirements planning, and input/output control.

Service Continuity Management is part of the overall management system that establishes, implements, operates, monitors, reviews, maintains, and improves an organization’s capability of delivering products or services at acceptable predefined levels following a disruptive incident. It is based on identifying potential threats to an organization and the impact on business operations from those threats. The system provides a framework for building organizational resilience with the capability of an effective response that safeguards the interests of its key stakeholders, reputation, brand, and value-creating activities.

Service Knowledge Management Systems is an integrated approach (system) used by organizations to capture, share, develop, and use organizational knowledge. This information is used to produce products, interface with customers, and navigate through competitive markets more effectively.

Service Validation and Testing Management is the practice of validating and testing new or changed services. Service validation and testing ensure that the service matches its design specification and will meet the needs of the business.

Service Valuation Management is the practice of measuring the total cost of delivering a service and the total value to the business of that service. Service valuation is used to help the business and the service provider agree on the value of the service.

Service Design Management is the practice of designing services, governing practices, processes, and policies required to realize the service provider’s strategy and to facilitate the introduction of services into supported environments. Service design management includes design coordination, service catalog management, service level management, capacity management, continuity management, information security management, and supplier management.

Service Transition Management is the practice of ensuring that new, modified, or retired services meet the expectation of the business as documented in the service strategy and service design stages of the lifecycle. Service transition management includes transition planning and support, change management, service asset and configuration management, release and deployment management, service validation and testing, change evaluation, and knowledge management.

Service Problem Management is the practice of managing the lifecycle of all service problems. Service problem management proactively prevents incidents from happening and minimizes the impact of incidents that cannot be prevented.

Continual Service Improvement ensures that services are aligned with changing business needs by identifying and implementing improvements to services that support business processes. The performance of the service provider is continually measured, and improvements are made to processes, services, and infrastructure in order to increase efficiency, effectiveness, and cost-effectiveness.

Dynamic Case Management is handling case-related work using technologies that automate and streamline aspects of each case. In this context, a case is a collection of information about a particular instance of something, such as a person, company, incident, or problem. It is the ability to have exceptions to the rule that enables smart decisions faster when handling ad-hoc workloads.

A Business Rules Management System (BRMS) utilizes Rules engines that are tools that support the identification, definition, rationalization, and quality of business and technology rules. Rules engines also provide a repository that allows rules to be checked against one another or definition or context problems and thus checked for redundancy and definition quality. In practice, rules are looked at as if-then statements: if (an event or value), then do something. Various classes of business rules include mandatory constraint, guideline, action enabler, computation, and inference.

Green Procurement is a technique used by a supply chain that considers environmental impacts on its operations and takes action along the supply chain to comply with environmental safety regulations and communicate this to customers and partners is considered a green supply chain.

Green procurement extends to the green supply chain aspect to consider the supplier selection criteria based on environmental standards, prequalifying suppliers based on environmental practices, auditing suppliers based on green practices, and drafting specifications with environmental aspects on it.

Usually, green and ethical procurement is an extension of the company strategy; organizations recently had been committing to the SDG's "Sustainable development goals' which cascaded to the procurement function.

Ethical Procurement is the practice of incorporating ethical standards into the procurement process. 'Ethics' in procurement relates to a wide range of issues from supplier business procedures and practices to corruption. The common areas relate to ethics and ethical behavior in companies include fair trade, ethical trading, ethical sourcing, social accountability, social auditing, corporate social responsibility, corporate citizenship, codes of conduct, and reputation assurance.

Early Supplier Involvement is the process of involving suppliers early in the product design activity and drawing on their expertise, insights, and knowledge to generate better designs in less time and designs that are easier to manufacture with high quality. See: participative design/engineering.

In-Country Value is a sustainable practice that aims to boost economic performance and support local industries by redirecting higher portions of spending into the national economy. This means that in the solicitation process, a local supplier will be given preference over international suppliers by assigning weight "Varies" to local suppliers in the comparison and awarding process. This does not necessarily mean awarding local suppliers always but rather emphasizing the empowerment of national suppliers. This practice helps the strategic localization of supply chains and the development of new local industries and services, Creating valuable job opportunities in the private sector & National GDP Growth.

Negotiations Planning is the practice of thoroughly preparing for negotiation with suppliers in advance, including research, knowing the objectives, understanding the concessions, and having a BATNA. It also includes:

Determining reasons for negotiation.
Economic analysis, including price, cost, and breakeven analysis.
The source of power for buyer and supplier in the negotiation process
How much resource should be used with negotiation preparation?
Preparing a negotiation Check List to enable a buyer to be certain that all generic aspects that could present themselves in a negotiation have been thought about as well as researched prior to the negotiation itself.
Determining negotiation styles (Collaborating, accommodating, competing, avoiding, compromising) as they vary depending on the relationship that a procurement professional has with their supplier and situationally in the procuring context.
Preparing negotiation ploys & tactics that are often used but can be subject to risks. Ploys/tactics must be carefully researched prior to introducing them into a negotiation.
Determining "MIL" The MUST, LIKE & INTEND by recording what must be achieved, what would be beneficial and what would be a bonus, a procurement professional can have a full overview of the areas that they are able to trade or concede on.
BATNA - A best alternative to a negotiated agreement.
What If Scenarios - if negotiation fails. It is not always possible to reach an agreement. If the negotiation cannot conclude in an acceptable manner, what are the options for escalation?

Contract Drafting is the process where upon setting specifications and building a business case, the procurement team will determine the contract particulars and what needs to be included in the contract for this specific procurement process.

Such as what type of payment is needed and what incoterm is preferred, delivery time, and other factors set in the specification drafting.

Usually, this happens with stakeholders in mind and prior to supplier selection or sourcing the market.

A Framework Agreement is the practice of making an agreement with suppliers, a framework agreement is a general term for agreements with suppliers which sets out terms and conditions under which specific purchases (call-offs) can be made throughout the term of the agreement.

This framework agreement may, itself, be a contract to which procurement rules apply. This would be the case where the agreement places an obligation, in writing, to purchase goods, works, or services.

It does not mean actual prices should be fixed, but rather that there should be a mechanism that will be applied to pricing particular requirements during the period of the framework. It should also be possible to establish the scope and types of goods and/or services that will need to be called off. There should not be any objection to upgrading the product or service required so long as it remains within the scope of the original specification.

Upon determining the need to procure, Procurement can create direct call-off or mini competition between the suppliers that had the framework agreement signed. Procurement also can buy the same goods/service from outside the framework agreement suppliers if deemed appropriate.

Supply Market Research is the practice of conducting supply market research enables procurement to understand how the supply market works, the direction in which the market is going, the competitiveness, and the key suppliers within the supply market.

The results of this analysis can help the buyer to improve and shape the strategy and tendering process and align their behavior in order to achieve better value for money, reduced prices, or improved service.

Effective procurement requires researching the supply markets and the competitive factors that affect these markets. Tools like Porter's five forces model and STEEPLE analysis can come in handy.

Porter’s five forces analysis can provide a useful framework for understanding these issues:

1. degree of competition

2. threat of new entrants

3. threat of substitute products and services.

4. the power of buyers

5. the power of suppliers

STEEPLED Analysis is a strategic planning methodology that can be used across all business functions to discover, evaluate, organize, and track external risk. It is an acronym, the individual letters standing for: Social, Technological, Economic, Environmental, Political, Legislative, Ethical, and Demographic.

Use STEEPLED analysis to identify the potential influence or disruption that the following macro (External) factors can have on your organization's activities, and having awareness of possible external disruptions, enables the organization to take a proactive approach and re-align elements or activities of their supply chain to enable them to continue to meet their business objectives.

Specification Development is the practice of specifying and documenting the business requirements for supply, specification is a systematic statement of the requirements to be satisfied in the supply of a product or service and sits at the heart of the contract between the buyer and the seller. A specification is developed to define the business requirements clearly and communicate these to suppliers effectively to facilitate the evaluation of goods and services against the agreed specification. An effective specification provides evidence of what is agreed upon and removes any doubt, ambiguity, or misunderstanding as to what is required.

Developing a detailed specification can be a timely and costly exercise, and there is a need to engage the necessary stakeholders and main users of the product or service to ensure an effective specification is created. During the specification development process, procurement must take steps to ensure the product is not being over-specified and the agreed tolerances are achievable so as not to add cost to the product and leave the organization exposed to too many restrictions on supply.

The implications of not developing an effective specification can be misunderstandings with key stakeholders and with the supplier over the requirements. This exposes the business requirement to interpretation or being over-specified or even inferior goods being delivered with defects or inconsistent quality.

An effective specification is clear, concise, comprehensive, compliant, and current to ensure there is no ambiguity with regard to the business requirements.

As stakeholders play an important part in effective specification development, the Stakeholder Management Matrix helps procurement to identify the key stakeholders to engage in the communication loop and development of the specification. The Early Supplier Involvement (ESI) Matrix helps procurement to establish how best to engage suppliers in the development process and the appropriate time relative to specific developments. Working in collaboration with suppliers in developing the specification and utilizing their expertise can often help to reduce the lead time and improve the quality.

A Blanket Agreement is the practice of signing a long-term commitment, most often annually, with a supplier of material/service against which short-term releases will be generated to satisfy requirements. Often blanket orders cover only one item. Blanket orders are indefinite by their nature, which means the dates of delivery and quantity notices from suppliers might not be fixed or known. Requirements are “based on demand.” Procurement would forecast the total demand needed and create a blanket agreement for that amount.

The payment progress is negotiable between parties in the blanket order, this means it might be based on individual deliveries or predetermined, like advanced payment or deferred payment.

Sustainable Specification Development is the practice of specifying and documenting the business requirements for supply using sustainable standards, A sustainable specification is developed to define the ethical and environmental business requirements clearly and communicate these to suppliers effectively to facilitate the evaluation of goods and services against the agreed specification.

Such specification would be a reflection of the organization's commitment to creating a sustainable business from an ethical and environmental standpoint. An example of such specification is the use of Eco-friendly products, the reduction of emissions, the use of recycled material, energy-efficient products, the acquisition of 14001 ISO standards.

A Supplier Certification Program manages the certification procedures verifying that a supplier operates, maintains, improves, and documents effective procedures that relate to the customer’s requirements. Such requirements can include cost, quality, delivery, flexibility, maintenance, safety, and ISO quality and environmental standards.

A Sustainable Procurement Strategy is a process whereby organizations meet their needs for goods, services, works, and utilities in a way that achieves value for money on a whole-life basis in terms of generating benefits not only to the organization but also to society and the economy, whilst minimizing damage to the environment.

To successfully take this into action, procurement should align the organization's sustainability strategy with the procurement strategy by:

1. Adopting a sustainable procurement strategy by establishing the role of procurement professionals and buyers, adopting the standards or targets showing what will and will not be bought, and agreeing on the techniques to be used.

2. Challenging the current culture within the company.

3. Publishing the sustainable procurement policy as a clear commitment to action and ensure that senior figures visibly pursue this policy and demonstrate their commitment to real action and change.

4. Developing a dialogue with suppliers: discuss with suppliers the possibility of a more sustainable version of current purchases.

Assurance of strategy implantation is instrumental and can be achieved through:

Benchmarking: comparing company practices (e.g., ethical sourcing or corporate social responsibility) with best-in-class performance.
Business alignment and stakeholder engagement: need to be measured to achieve a clear linkage between business strategy, goals, and sustainable procurement initiatives (Hughes and Day, 2011).

A Multi-Tier Supplier Audit is the practice of officially inspecting Suppliers' tiers by the buying organization or an independent third party to ensure compliance with requirements and standards.

Buyers can use questionnaires to gather information on suppliers' attitudes to ethical concerns and sustainable practices. Also, can be done by visiting supplier premises to judge if those multi-tiers of suppliers are adhering to sustainable practices. Usually, these audits are investigative by their nature, where buying organization seeks to find evidence of violations of human rights, for example.

Can be carried out by also interviewing employees of these suppliers, tour at the supplier workplace, face to face at the supplier's premises, and a structured series of questions that touch base with the contract signed to guarantee adherence.

Where possible, these visits and audits should be unannounced to prevent any sort of preparation at the place, such as cleaning, hazard removal, imposing safety, or the creation of new documentation.
An Approved Vendor List is a list of parties that have been approved by a company as its suppliers. This list usually is based on product quality and the financial stability of the vendor.

A Supplier Credit Check is a practice of researching whether the supplier is financially stable, one way to do this is to carry out a credit check with a credit rating agency. They collect information about suppliers from various resources and produce a score that reflects the financial stability of the supplier. A supplier with a low credit rating would impose risk on the buying organization. Procurement uses the credit check practice to understand supplier financial solvency and bankruptcy risk.

Alternatively, the procurement department can internally calculate supplier solvency using measures like Altman Z Score, Gearing Ratios, Liquidity & profitability ratios of the suppliers using their financial statements.

The practice is instrumental to help In prequalifying suppliers and preparing an approved supplier list.
In marketing, Category Management provides an organizational structure for managers responsible for planning and implementing marketing systems for certain product lines.

Specification Value Analysis is the systematic use of techniques that identify a required function, establish a value for that function, and provides that function at the lowest overall cost. Focuses on the functions of an item rather than the methods of producing the present product design.

Specification Value Engineering is a disciplined approach to the elimination of waste from products or processes through an investigative process that focuses on the functions to be performed and whether such functions add value to the good or service.
A Make Or Buy Analysis is a comparison of all the costs associated with making an item versus the cost of buying the item.

Outsourcing is the process of having suppliers provide goods and services that were previously provided internally. Outsourcing involves substitution—the replacement of internal capacity and production by that of the supplier. See: subcontracting.

Open Tendering is the practice of widely advertising a tender to be available for any supplier to make a bid, which can be through journals, websites, mass communication, social media, or e-procurement portals.

In some instances, suppliers must express their interest to obtain the ITT "Invitation to tender."

Restricted Tendering is the practice of restricting advertising a tender to be available for a few suppliers to make a bid, which can be through inviting suppliers from the existing database or from the approved supplier's list or prequalified suppliers.

In some instances, suppliers must express their interest to obtain the ITT "Invitation to tender"

The Tendring process should avoid conflict of interest, should be run in an ethical and sustainable way, and a formalized arrangement should be in place.
A Reverse Auction is an internet auction in which suppliers attempt to underbid their competitors. Company identities are known only by the buyer.
Spot Buying is a purchase made on a one-time basis for standard off-the-shelf material or equipment.

Trade Exchanges are the practice of using web-based marketplaces "Platforms" to procure goods and services, Trade exchanges are either hosted by third parties or hosted by the buying organization to facilitate a collaborative procurement process with upstream partners.

The goal is to streamline the procurement process and responsiveness through improved procurement process visibility and collaboration, advanced integration platforms, and customization capabilities.

As an increasing number of companies embed digital strategies from the top down, B2B Marketplaces are becoming a familiar component within the procurement toolkit.

Trade exchanges offer a range of capabilities that connects sellers with buyers, for example, wholesale companies and end customers. A third-party marketplace offers users an interface to the supplier’s product catalogs and may additionally support payment, logistics, or ordering.

E-catalog management is the practice that enables buying organizations to procure goods/services electronically via the electronic product content (e-catalog) made available by suppliers. The product content can be hosted by either the supplier or the buyer.

This web-based technology provides information on products and services offered and sold by a vendor, Supports online ordering and payment capabilities. Key elements of a catalog are product names, product hierarchy, descriptions, prices, and supplier and internal codes.

E-catalogs are predominantly used for procuring frequently replenished indirect goods and services but may also provide purchasing guidelines to facilitate complicated procurements.

A Continuous Replenishment Program is a process by which a supplier is notified daily of actual sales or warehouse shipments and commits to replenishing these sales (for example, by size or color) without stockouts and without receiving replenishment orders. The result is a lowering of associated costs and an improvement in inventory turnover. See: rapid replenishment, vendor-managed inventory.

A Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) Analysis is the analysis of the total cost of ownership of the supply delivery system is the sum of all the costs associated with every activity of the supply stream. The main insight that TCO offers to the supply chain manager is the understanding that the acquisition cost is often a very small portion of the total cost of ownership.

A Price Analysis is the examination of a seller’s price proposal or bid by comparison with price benchmarks, without examination and evaluation of all of the separate elements of the cost and profit making up the price in the bid.

A Purchase Price Cost Analysis is the practice of analyzing the cost of the individual materials, components, and activities that make up a purchased item.

Purchase price cost analysis is one way to analyze prices offered by the supplier with the purpose of understanding how the price sums up with cost elements, this helps the buyers better negotiate with their suppliers.

It also helps answer key questions such as

- Is the price paid for goods and services reasonable?

- Which costs are necessary and legitimate?

- Are there any cost additions or allowances for contingencies in the pricing that is not necessary?

- Are the resulting profits for the supplier reasonable or excessive?

Supplier Debriefing is the practice of informing suppliers about the status of the tender awarding and whether they were awarded or not, Supplier debriefings are an integral part of a transparent and equitable procurement process which permits unsuccessful suppliers in an open call for bids an opportunity to understand why their bid was not successful.

Debriefing is a way of helping suppliers to improve their competitive performance which produces benefits to procuring organizations.

MEAT Awarding (Most Economically Advantageous Tender) is the practice of evaluating and awarding suppliers where procurement takes account of criteria that reflect qualitative, technical, and sustainable aspects of the tender submission as well as price when reaching an award decision.

Most Economically Advantageous Tender means the Tender offer that is most economically advantageous regarding the subject matter of the contract, such as quality, price, technical merit, aesthetic and functional characteristics, environmental characteristics, running costs, cost-effectiveness, after-sales service, technical assistance, delivery date and delivery period or period of completion and other matters.

The relative weighting of each criterion used to assess the submissions must be determined with scoring to reach an awarding decision.

A Solicitation Process is a practice used by procurement to communicate procurement requirements and request bids, quotations, or proposals from potential suppliers. Solicitations may take different forms such as Request for Quotation (RFQ), Invitation to Bid (ITB), or Request for Proposal (RFP).

A Purchase Price arrangement is a practice of determining the appropriate cost/price contracting mechanism that governs price & cost changes during the life of the contract.

Depending on the nature of work and type of goods/services procured, Procurement would consider the appropriate purchase price arrangements.

There are many arrangements that can be considered upon contracting such as:

- Firm Fixed-price

- Fixed price with economic Adjustment

- Cost plus fixed fee

- Cost reimbursement

- Cost plus %

Each one of them imposes a different degree of risks on the buying organizations, for example, A Firm Fixed-price has the lowest risk as it prevents changes to the original price contracted no matter what changes take place in the cost structure at the supplier side.

Progress Payments are payments arranged in connection with purchase transactions requiring periodic payments in advance of delivery for certain amounts or for certain percentages of the purchase price.

Single Sourcing is a method whereby a purchased part is supplied by only one supplier. Traditional manufacturers usually have at least two suppliers for each component part they purchase to ensure continuity of supply and (more so) to foster price competition between the suppliers. A JIT manufacturer frequently has only one supplier for a purchased part so close relationships can be established with a smaller number of suppliers. These close relationships (and mutual interdependence) foster high quality, reliability, short lead times, and cooperative action. Ant: multisourcing. See: sole source.
Dual Sourcing is a method for sourcing requirements by using a few suppliers for the same products or services. See: multisourcing, multiple sourcing, single sourcing.

Portfolio Analysis is the practice of segmenting sourcing into four categories so that the appropriate level of management attention and resources can be applied to the sourcing and procurement processes.

This model can be used to determine which suppliers are most appropriate for each of the four types of goods or services:

Commodity materials and services are of low strategic importance and low supply chain difficulty. They require suppliers whose priority is cost reduction. These items are best purchased at arm’s length with little negotiation. A key strategy here is to simplify and automate the procurement process for these categories. Rationalizing or right-sizing the supply base is also important.
Bottleneck materials and services are of low strategic importance but are of high supply chain difficulty. A key strategy is to ensure that the need for these items is fulfilled. Therefore, some level of ongoing relationship with a particular supplier may be vital. Another goal can be to eliminate the bottleneck by finding or developing more potential suppliers.
Leverageable materials and services have high strategic importance but low difficulty. The key strategy for these high-purchase-volume materials is to determine a set of preferred suppliers one can work with over time to get high and increasing levels of quality, service, objectives compliance, and cost improvement. one should maintain a healthy amount of competition. Other options include exploiting market cycles or bulk purchasing by multiple members of the supply chain.
Direct/core competency materials and services are of high strategic importance and high difficulty. The key strategy for these goods and services is to form strategic partnerships for longer periods of time to ensure availability and quality. This area requires detailed negotiations for contracts and contingency plans.

Supplier Segmentation is a practice that organizes the relationship with suppliers by positioning them into different segments based on many parameters, suppliers in each category can have transactional, preferred, strategic, or ownership relationships.

Supplier segments range across a spectrum of buyer-supplier relationships. At one end of the spectrum is the traditional transactional supplier segment, or “buy on the market.” The next segment is preferred suppliers. The strategic relationship segment needs to be a core supplier.

Another approach to segmenting suppliers would be a 20:80 approach where some suppliers are classed A, others are B, and C depending on the among of spend and the type of material.

Supply Base Rightsizing or rationalization involves a review of the suppliers in a category to determine the ideal number. Usually, this involves finding categories with too many suppliers and reducing that number by awarding the business to fewer, more preferred suppliers.

Rightsizing can improve the quality of remaining suppliers or get quantity discounts, reducing administrative costs. Ordering costs and supplier relationship management costs. More time can be spent on each supplier when fewer suppliers exist, and this can enable more collaborative relationships.

Pareto analysis can be used, and the top 20 percent of suppliers by category spend could be those retained. A set of more rigid supplier requirements could be rolled out to all suppliers with an ultimatum to meet the requirements or be dropped. A triage approach could be used to evaluate suppliers and place them into categories such as unacceptable, minimum qualifying, and world-class performance. other organizational goals might also be accommodated, such as prioritizing the use of local suppliers or retaining suppliers who meet sustainability objectives.
